full_name: Executive Order on the Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: None — Executive order; no penalty regime. Revoked by EO 14179.
preemption_notes: Executive order; revoked by EO 14179
summary: Biden's landmark 2023 AI executive order directed federal agencies to develop safety standards, required developers of powerful AI systems to share safety test results with the government, and tasked NIST with creating AI risk benchmarks. It addressed everything from AI in hiring to biosecurity risks and was the most comprehensive US federal AI governance action prior to its revocation.
notable: Revoked by EO 14179 on January 20, 2025. Most directives expired with the administration; some NIST frameworks and agency rules derived from it remain in effect.
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,110, 88 Fed. Reg. 75,191 (Nov. 1, 2023)
key_obligations: Frontier AI developers with training compute above threshold must share safety test results with NIST
NIST to develop AI risk management benchmarks and red-teaming standards
Federal agencies must conduct AI risk assessments before procurement
OMB to issue binding guidance on government AI use and procurement

impact_assessment.detail: Required frontier model developers (training compute ≥10²⁶ FLOP) to share safety test results with the government before deployment; tasked NIST with developing AI risk benchmarks.

prohibited_categories.detail: Executive order did not prohibit specific AI applications, instead directing agency rulemaking.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights to human review; directed agencies to study AI in high-stakes decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Executive order; no private enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: Directed NIST and DHS to develop authentication and watermarking standards for AI-generated content.

biometric_data.detail: Did not address biometric data specifically.

training_data_transparency.detail: Did not require public disclosure of training datasets.

content_labeling.detail: Directed NIST to develop watermarking guidance and required OSTP to develop a National Strategy for AI watermarking.

anti_discrimination.detail: Directed EEOC, DOJ, and FTC to issue guidance applying existing civil rights laws to AI; created no new anti-discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: Used dual-use foundation model training compute threshold (≥10²⁶ FLOP) to define reporting and safety obligations.

enforcement_model.detail: Agency directives only; no penalty structure or enforcement mechanism.

operative_dates: Signed 30 Oct 2023. Agency-specific deadlines ranged from 30 to 365 days. Revoked in its entirety by EO 14179 (20 Jan 2025).

full_name: Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: None — Executive order; no penalty regime. Directs agency action but imposes no fines.
summary: EO 14179 revoked the Biden AI Executive Order and directed agencies to develop an 'AI Action Plan' prioritizing US dominance in AI over safety-focused regulation. It ordered review and removal of federal AI policies inconsistent with promoting AI innovation and directed OSTP to coordinate a national AI strategy emphasizing competitiveness.
notable: Revoked EO 14110 on day one of Trump administration. Marks major shift from safety-focused to competitiveness-focused federal AI policy.
legal_citation: Exec. Order No. 14,179, 90 Fed. Reg. 8,741 (Jan. 31, 2025)
key_obligations: Agencies to review and revoke Biden-era AI policies inconsistent with innovation priority
OSTP and OSTP to develop AI Action Plan prioritizing US AI dominance
Remove regulatory barriers to AI development and deployment

impact_assessment.detail: Revoked Biden-era safety mandates; directed agencies to eliminate AI regulations deemed to impede innovation.

prohibited_categories.detail: Deregulatory in nature; no prohibited-use categories.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: Did not address AI-generated content authentication.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions.

anti_discrimination.detail: Did not address anti-discrimination in AI contexts.

risk_classification.detail: Removed compute-threshold and risk-tier framework from EO 14110; directed development of an AI Action Plan prioritizing competitiveness.

enforcement_model.detail: Agency directives only; deregulatory stance.

full_name: Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks Act
max_penalty: Criminal: up to 2 years imprisonment per violation; civil damages
preemption_notes: Preempts inconsistent state laws on non-consensual intimate imagery
summary: The TAKE IT DOWN Act requires online platforms to remove non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII), including AI-generated deepfake sexual images, within 48 hours of a valid takedown request. It criminalizes the publication of such content and tasks the FTC with enforcement. The first federal law specifically targeting AI-generated deepfake pornography.
notable: First US federal statute specifically targeting AI-generated intimate imagery. Signed by President Trump.
key_obligations: Platforms must remove non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) including AI-generated within 48 hours of valid request
Criminal prohibition on publishing NCII
FTC to enforce against non-compliant platforms under Section 5

impact_assessment.detail: Targeted criminal statute; no impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits publication of non-consensual intimate AI-generated images (NCII/deepfakes), specifically targeting synthetic sexual content.

human_review_rights.detail: No human review rights; focuses on criminal prohibition and platform takedown.

private_right_of_action.detail: Victims may seek injunctive relief and actual damages, including emotional distress, from publishers and non-compliant platforms.

synthetic_media.detail: Criminalizes publication of NCII deepfakes, provides civil remedy, and requires platforms to take down reported content within 48 hours.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric data provisions.

content_labeling.detail: No labeling requirements; focuses on prohibition and removal.

anti_discrimination.detail: Not an anti-discrimination law; targets sexual exploitation.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework.

enforcement_model.detail: Federal criminal offense (up to 2 years imprisonment) plus civil damages for victims and $50,000 civil penalties for non-compliant platforms.

background.origin: The TAKE IT DOWN Act (Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Nurturing the Development and Enforcement of Walled Gardening in Our Nation) was a direct legislative response to the epidemic of AI-generated NCII affecting minors on social media platforms. It extended the civil framework of the DEFIANCE Act with criminal penalties and mandatory platform takedown obligations, closing the gap left by the DEFIANCE Act's civil-only approach. First Lady Melania Trump publicly championed the bill, making it a signature initiative of the Trump administration's AI safety agenda.
key_advocates: Melania Trump (Be Best campaign successor initiative)
National Center for Missing and Exploited Children
key_opposition: Electronic Frontier Foundation (overbroad takedown regime)
ACLU (First Amendment concerns about mandatory removal)
unique_features: First federal statute to impose criminal penalties (fines plus up to 2 years imprisonment) for publishing AI-generated NCII
First federal law to impose mandatory 48-hour takedown obligation on online platforms for AI-generated NCII
Championed by a sitting First Lady — Melania Trump's most prominent policy initiative
Covers both real and synthetic (AI-generated) intimate imagery, closing the gap in prior laws that only covered non-synthetic imagery
Creates an independent cause of action separate from DEFIANCE Act
background.legislative_notes: Passed the Senate unanimously (99-0) in February 2025. House passage in March 2025 with strong bipartisan support. Signed by President Trump on April 28, 2025. The unanimous Senate passage reflected the rare political salience of child protection + AI deepfakes issue. First Lady Melania Trump attended the signing ceremony, marking her most prominent public policy moment of the second Trump term.

full_name: Consumer Protections for Artificial Intelligence Act
max_penalty: $20,000 per violation
preemption_notes: State law; no preemption clause but subject to federal preemption risk
summary: Colorado's landmark risk-based AI law requires developers and deployers of 'high-risk AI' systems to use reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination. Mandates impact assessments, consumer notifications of AI use, documentation of decision-making, and annual reporting. Covers high-stakes domains: housing, lending, employment, education, healthcare, insurance.

key_obligations: Deployers of high-risk AI must use reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination
Conduct and document algorithmic impact assessment before deployment
Notify consumers when high-risk AI is used in consequential decisions
Provide opportunity for consumers to appeal AI-assisted decisions
Developers must provide deployers with impact assessment documentation

background.origin: Colorado SB 205 emerged after the Colorado General Assembly observed the EU AI Act framework and sought to create the first comprehensive state-level AI governance statute in the US. The trigger was growing concern about automated decision-making in employment, insurance, credit, and healthcare following high-profile AEDT controversies in New York City (Local Law 144). Governor Jared Polis signed the bill in May 2024 but simultaneously sent a letter to the legislature calling for revisions before its 2026 effective date, signalling immediate political tension.
key_opposition: US Chamber of Commerce
Colorado Technology Association
Google
Amazon
Microsoft
BSA | The Software Alliance
unique_features: First US state law to adopt an EU-style risk-based framework with pre-deployment impact assessments
Governor who signed it simultaneously called for its revision before effective date — unprecedented self-undermining enactment
Defines "consequential decision" to cover employment, credit, housing, education, and healthcare AI
Requires algorithmic discrimination impact assessment filed with the state attorney general
Contains a "first in the nation" model for developer/deployer liability allocation that became a template for Texas TRAIGA and Washington's approach
background.legislative_notes: SB 205 passed the Colorado Senate 28-7 and the House 46-16. Polis signed it on May 17, 2024, while simultaneously sending a letter requesting the legislature reconvene to "make necessary improvements" before its February 1, 2026 effective date. A legislative workgroup was convened but its recommendations have not been enacted as of April 2026, creating significant uncertainty about whether the law will take effect as written.

operative_dates: Original effective date: 1 Feb 2026. Substantially amended by SB 25-318 (May 2025); revised obligations and extended compliance deadlines pending final enactment.

Requires state agencies and healthcare providers to disclose AI use in consumer-facing interactions. Exclusive AG enforcement with tiered penalties.
legal_citation: Tex. Bus. & Com. Code §§ 541.001–541.056 (TRAIGA); HB 149, 89th Leg.
key_obligations: Prohibit AI designed to induce self-harm or generate CSAM
Prohibit AI-generated deepfake pornography
Prohibit social credit scoring AI systems
State agencies and healthcare providers must disclose AI use in consumer interactions
AG enforcement with tiered civil penalties

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits AI that generates CSAM, facilitates social credit scoring for coercive government control, and manipulates users into self-harm or suicide.

human_review_rights.detail: Consumers may appeal consequential AI decisions to a human reviewer; deployers must provide a meaningful appeals process within specific timeframes.

biometric_data.detail: Not specifically addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Applies to "high-risk AI systems" in consequential decisions across 6 listed domains; excludes B2B and small business exemptions.

enforcement_model.detail: AG civil penalties up to $200,000 per violation; injunctive relief available.

full_name: Indiana Health Benefit Claims — AI Limitation Act
summary: Prohibits health insurers from using fully automated AI processes to submit or deny health benefit claims without human review by a qualified provider or claims professional. Ensures human accountability in AI-assisted health insurance claim adjudication.
key_obligations: Health insurers may not use fully automated AI to adjudicate claims without human review
Claims must be reviewed by qualified provider or licensed claims professional
Human override required before issuing AI-generated claim denials

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits health insurance companies from using AI to automatically deny claims without individual medical necessity review by a licensed clinician.

human_review_rights.detail: All AI-generated health insurance coverage denials must be reviewed and approved by a licensed clinician before becoming final; no purely automated claim denials permitted.

private_right_of_action.detail: IDOI enforcement; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Sector-specific (health insurance) only; no general risk tier.

enforcement_model.detail: IDOI enforcement; license suspension, civil penalties for violations.

full_name: Oregon Conversational AI Disclosure Act
max_penalty: $1,000 per violation (statutory damages)
summary: Requires conversational AI operators to clearly disclose to users that they are interacting with an AI system. Includes a private right of action with statutory damages of $1,000 per violation, making it notable for providing a private enforcement mechanism.
notable: Private right of action distinguishes this from most state chatbot disclosure laws.
legal_citation: ORS § 646A.810; SB 1546, 2026 Ore. Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Conversational AI operators must clearly disclose that users are interacting with AI
Disclosure required at start of interaction and upon sincere user request
Private right of action: $1,000 per violation, class actions permitted

impact_assessment.detail: Disclosure-only law.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: $1,000 statutory damages per violation for non-disclosure; private right of action.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: AI systems must disclose AI nature when sincerely asked; applies to consumer-facing chatbots.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: $1,000/violation with private right of action; AG enforcement.

full_name: Idaho Conversational AI Safety Act
max_penalty: $1,000 per violation (up to $500,000 per operator)
summary: Requires conversational AI operators to disclose AI interaction to users, particularly minors. Prohibits generating sexually explicit content or content simulating romantic relationships with minors. Mandates crisis referral protocols when suicidal ideation is detected.
legal_citation: Idaho Code §§ 48-1801 to 48-1808; SB 1297, 2026 Idaho Leg.
key_obligations: Disclose AI identity to users, especially minors
Prohibit generating sexually explicit content or simulating romantic relationships with minors
Implement crisis referral protocols when suicidal ideation is detected
Penalty: $1,000 per violation, up to $500,000 per operator

max_penalty: $1,000 per violation (up to $500,000 per operator)
summary: Requires conversational AI chatbot operators to disclose AI identity to users, prohibit CSAM generation, mandate crisis referral protocols, and restrict romantic/sexual interactions with minors. Mirrors Idaho's approach with identical penalty structure.
key_obligations: Disclose AI identity at start of user interaction
Prohibit CSAM generation
Mandate crisis referral protocols
Restrict romantic/sexual interactions with minors
Penalty: $1,000 per violation, up to $500,000 per operator

full_name: Act to Regulate the Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Provision of Mental Health Services
enforcement_body: Maine Office of Professional and Financial Regulation
max_penalty: $10,000 per violation
summary: Prohibits unlicensed entities from offering therapy services using AI and restricts licensed practitioners to administrative AI use only with client consent. AI systems may not be deployed to provide psychotherapy or mental health counseling services without licensed professional supervision.
legal_citation: Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 32, § 18295; LD 2082, 132nd Me. Leg. (2026)
key_obligations: Prohibit unlicensed entities from offering therapy using AI
Licensed practitioners may only use AI for administrative tasks with client consent
AI may not provide psychotherapy without licensed professional supervision
Penalty: $10,000 per violation

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits unlicensed AI from providing mental health counseling or therapy services to Maine consumers; requires licensed professional oversight.

human_review_rights.detail: AI mental health tools must be supervised by licensed therapists; AI may not operate autonomously in therapeutic relationships.

private_right_of_action.detail: Licensing board enforcement.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: AI-based mental health tools must identify as AI; users must know they are interacting with AI.

full_name: Protection From Predatory Pricing Act
enforcement_body: Maryland Office of the Attorney General
max_penalty: Consumer protection civil penalties
summary: Prohibits food retailers and grocery delivery services from using personal consumer data to set individualized (surveillance-based) pricing. First state law banning algorithmic price discrimination at grocery stores. Applies to retailers with $100M+ annual revenue.
legal_citation: Md. Code, Com. Law § 11-501 et seq. (as amended); HB 895, 2026 Md. Gen. Assem.
key_obligations: Food retailers ($100M+ revenue) prohibited from using personal consumer data to set individualized prices
Prohibit using purchase history or location data for price discrimination
AG enforcement; consumer civil penalties

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits landlords and property managers from using AI algorithms to coordinate or fix rental prices; treats algorithmic rent coordination as a consumer protection violation.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Tenants harmed by algorithmic rent coordination may sue for damages and injunctive relief.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

anti_discrimination.detail: Algorithmic pricing prohibition intersects with fair housing law; defers to existing anti-discrimination framework.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: AG enforcement; civil penalties plus private right of action.

full_name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act
max_penalty: $1,000–$5,000 per violation (statutory damages)
preemption_notes: Model for other state biometric laws
summary: Requires private entities collecting biometric identifiers (fingerprints, retinal scans, facial geometry, voiceprints) to obtain written consent, establish retention policies, and prohibits selling biometric data. Provides private right of action with statutory damages per violation. Highly relevant to AI facial recognition and voice AI systems.
notable: Pre-AI era law that became the primary US litigation vehicle for AI biometric claims (2008). Multiple major class actions with nine-figure settlements.
legal_citation: 740 ILCS 14/1 et seq. (Biometric Information Privacy Act); 2008 Ill. Laws 95-994
key_obligations: Prior written consent required before collecting biometric identifiers
Publicly available written policy with retention schedule and destruction guidelines
No sale or profit from biometric data
Destroy data when purpose is fulfilled or 3 years, whichever first
Private right of action: $1,000–$5,000 per violation; class actions permitted

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed; BIPA predates AI-specific impact assessment frameworks.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited categories per se; consent requirements effectively restrict biometric collection.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: $1,000 per negligent violation and $5,000 per intentional/reckless violation; no actual harm required; class actions routinely certified.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Requires written consent before collection, published retention policy, prohibition on sale, and destruction within 3 years or when purpose is fulfilled; backed by per-violation statutory damages.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal penalties (Class A misdemeanor), statutory civil damages ($1K–$5K/violation), and class actions certified without actual harm showing — the most aggressive enforcement model in US law.

background.origin: Prompted by rapid expansion of private biometric database collection by employers (finger-scan timekeeping), gyms, and amusement parks following adoption of fingerprint technology for employee check-in in the mid-2000s, with no legal framework for consent, deletion, or sale restrictions.
key_opposition: Illinois Retail Merchants Association
Illinois Chamber of Commerce
Amusement park operators and employers using biometric timekeeping
unique_features: Private right of action with statutory damages ($1,000–$5,000 per violation) requiring no proof of actual harm — unique globally
First US law to mandate biometric data deletion schedule
Four independent obligations: consent, written policy, no-sale, destruction
Class action eligibility has driven billions in settlements (Facebook $650M, TikTok $92M, BNSF Railway $228M)
Treats each scan as a separate violation, enabling catastrophic per-incident liability
background.legislative_notes: Passed in a single 2008 Illinois legislative session with little public debate; significance not recognised until 2015–2017 class action wave. Illinois Supreme Court in Rosenbach v. Six Flags (2019) confirmed no actual harm required for standing. Amendments narrowed one-year limitations period in 2024 (PA 103-0769) following catastrophic employer liability concerns.

full_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: €35M or 7% global annual turnover (prohibited AI); €15M or 3% (high-risk non-compliance); €7.5M or 1% (misleading info)
preemption_notes: EU Regulation directly applicable in all 27 member states; no lower legislation may conflict
summary: The world's first binding horizontal AI regulation establishes a risk-based framework: prohibited AI practices (social scoring, mass biometric surveillance, manipulation) banned from Feb 2025; high-risk AI (healthcare, employment, critical infrastructure) requires conformity assessment, registration, and human oversight from Aug 2025; general-purpose AI models face transparency obligations; full enforcement August 2026.
notable: Reference instrument globally. Phased implementation: prohibited AI Feb 2, 2025; high-risk/GPAI Aug 2, 2025; full enforcement Aug 2, 2026.
legal_citation: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council, O.J. L 2024/1689
key_obligations: Prohibited practices: real-time biometric surveillance in public, social scoring, manipulation of subliminal vulnerabilities
High-risk AI systems must undergo conformity assessment before market placement
General-purpose AI models (GPAI) with significant systemic risk require safety evaluations
Providers must maintain technical documentation and register in EU AI database
Deployers must conduct fundamental rights impact assessment for certain high-risk uses
EU AI Office to supervise GPAI models; national supervisory authorities for other systems

impact_assessment.detail: High-risk AI systems require conformity assessment (Annex VI) before market placement; many high-risk systems require notified body involvement for third-party conformity verification.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits real-time biometric surveillance in public, social scoring, manipulation exploiting vulnerabilities, predictive policing based on profiling, emotion recognition in workplaces/schools, and scraping facial images for databases.

human_review_rights.detail: High-risk AI deployers must ensure human oversight; individuals subject to high-risk AI decisions have the right to explanation and to request human review under Art. 86.

private_right_of_action.detail: No direct private right of action in the AI Act; civil liability channeled through EU AI Liability Directive and EU PLD companion legislation treating AI as defective product.

synthetic_media.detail: GPAI models must watermark AI-generated content (Art. 50); deepfakes must be labeled; providers must implement state-of-the-art provenance detection.

biometric_data.detail: Prohibits deploying real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement except under narrow judicial authorization.

training_data_transparency.detail: Providers must file technical documentation including training data governance with national market surveillance authorities and the EU AI Office; not public.

content_labeling.detail: GPAI model providers must mark AI-generated content with machine-readable watermarks; deployers using GPAI in consumer-facing products must label synthetic content to users.

anti_discrimination.detail: High-risk deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIA) before deployment; assessment must cover protected characteristics and rights.

risk_classification.detail: Four-tier system: unacceptable risk (prohibited), high-risk (full compliance), limited risk (transparency only), minimal risk (voluntary code); applies to all AI systems placed on the EU market.

enforcement_model.detail: Up to €35M or 7% global annual turnover for prohibited-use violations; EU AI Office oversight; coordinated with EU PLD for civil liability.

background.origin: Triggered by the 2019 EU High-Level Expert Group on AI white paper and the European Commission's 2020 White Paper on AI; accelerated by societal concern over facial recognition, predictive policing, and biased automated decision systems revealed in the late 2010s. The Commission published its first proposal in April 2021.
key_opposition: DigitalEurope (industry lobbied for narrower prohibited list)
Mistral AI and European tech companies (lobbied for GPAI carve-outs)
Several member state intelligence agencies (sought public security exemptions)
US tech companies via CCIA
unique_features: World's first comprehensive binding AI legislation with risk-tier architecture
Prohibited practices list including social scoring and real-time biometric surveillance in public
Conformity assessment obligations for high-risk systems placing burden on deployers
General-purpose AI (GPAI) model obligations including for frontier models above 10^25 FLOPs
EU AI Office as dedicated enforcement body — first of its kind globally
Extraterritorial effect: applies to systems affecting EU persons regardless of where developers are based
background.legislative_notes: Proposed April 2021; co-rapporteurs appointed Feb 2022; Parliament adopted its position June 2023 (adding GPAI chapter and stronger prohibited list); trilogue negotiations ran July–December 2023; political agreement December 8, 2023; formal adoption March 2024; entered force August 1, 2024. Phased implementation: prohibited practices February 2025, GPAI August 2025, high-risk obligations August 2026.

implementation_phases.description: EU AI Act enters into force
Prohibited practices (Art. 5) and general provisions apply; GPAI obligations begin
Notified body designation process opens; conformity assessment procedures applicable
High-risk AI obligations (Annex III) and transparency requirements fully apply
High-risk AI obligations for Annex I (regulated products) fully apply; AI systems embedded in regulated products

operative_dates: Prohibited systems ban: 2 Aug 2024. GPAI model rules & governance: 2 Aug 2025. High-risk system obligations (Annex I): 2 Aug 2026. High-risk system obligations (Annex II): 2 Aug 2027.

full_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 — General Data Protection Regulation (Automated Decision-Making Provisions)
max_penalty: €20M or 4% global annual turnover
preemption_notes: EU Regulation directly applicable in all 27 member states
summary: Article 22 GDPR grants individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions (including profiling) that produce legal or similarly significant effects. Requires human intervention, explanation, and contestation rights when exceptions apply. First major binding regulation of AI decision-making globally.
notable: Pre-AI era provision that became foundational to AI rights discourse. Enforced against algorithmic credit scoring, automated hiring tools, and targeted advertising.
legal_citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Art. 22, O.J. L 119/1 (May 4, 2016)
key_obligations: Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects
Data subject may request human review of automated decision
Controller must explain logic of automated decision upon request
Explicit consent required for profiling producing legal effects
Data protection impact assessment required for systematic automated processing

impact_assessment.detail: Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs) are mandatory for automated decision-making, large-scale biometric data processing, and other high-risk processing; DPIA must be completed before processing begins.

prohibited_categories.detail: GDPR does not prohibit specific AI applications; restricts lawfulness of data processing underlying AI systems.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 22 grants individuals the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions that produce legal or similarly significant effects; the broadest human review right globally.

private_right_of_action.detail: Art. 82 gives individuals the right to compensation for material or immaterial damage from GDPR violations; class representative action now available in most EU member states.

synthetic_media.detail: GDPR does not specifically address synthetic media; privacy rights may apply if real individuals are depicted.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is a special category (Art. 9); processing requires explicit consent or another Art. 9(2) condition; controllers bear heightened duty of care.

training_data_transparency.detail: GDPR does not specifically require training data disclosure; transparency obligations cover how personal data is processed, not training data composition.

anti_discrimination.detail: Art. 22 prohibits automated decisions based on special category data including race and religion; defers to national anti-discrimination law for substantive standard.

risk_classification.detail: GDPR predates AI risk classification frameworks; processing risk is assessed through DPIA, not AI system risk tiers.

enforcement_model.detail: Up to €20M or 4% global annual turnover for serious violations; DPA enforcement plus Art. 82 individual compensation right.

background.origin: Replaced the 1995 Data Protection Directive as the internet and big data transformed the scale of personal data processing; triggered by Edward Snowden revelations (2013) about mass surveillance, the Facebook/Cambridge Analytica concerns emerging by 2012–2014, and the single-market fragmentation caused by 28 different national data laws.
key_drafters: Jan Philipp Albrecht MEP (European Parliament rapporteur)
key_opposition: US tech industry (Google, Facebook, Microsoft, Amazon) lobbied heavily against extraterritoriality and consent requirements
UK ICO sought lighter enforcement model
Germany opposed single supervisory authority model
unique_features: Article 22 creates the first binding right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or significant effects — directly applicable to AI
Extraterritorial reach: applies to all processing of EU residents' data regardless of where processor is based
Maximum 4% of global annual turnover penalty — at the time the largest penalty regime globally
Right to explanation for automated decisions — debated but influential on AI explainability discourse
Data protection by design and by default — first codification of privacy engineering obligations
background.legislative_notes: Proposed January 2012; four-year negotiation including 3,999 amendments in Parliament (a record); agreed trilogue December 2015; formally adopted April 2016; applied May 25, 2018 (two-year transition). Became the de-facto global data protection standard, inspiring laws in 130+ jurisdictions.

operative_dates: Adopted Apr 2016; entered into force May 2016; applicable 25 May 2018 (two-year implementation grace period).

full_name: Interim Measures for the Administration of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services
enforcement_body: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology
max_penalty: Service suspension; warnings; enforcement under cybersecurity/PIPL frameworks
preemption_notes: National regulation issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC); provincial and local governments may not enact conflicting rules but may implement supplementary compliance requirements.
summary: China's first binding GenAI regulation requires CAC licensing before public deployment of large language models. Prohibits content violating socialist core values, mandates user registration, requires training data security and personal information protection, and mandates AI-generated content labelling. Security assessment required for LLMs before public release.
notable: First national binding regulation of generative AI globally, preceding the EU AI Act's GPAI provisions.
legal_citation: Interim Measures for the Management of Generative Artificial Intelligence Services, CAC/MIIT/MPS/MNR/PBC/SAMR No. 15 (2023)
key_obligations: AI-generated content must be labeled as AI-generated
Service providers must conduct security assessment before launch
Training data must not include prohibited content (defined broadly)
Providers responsible for content generated by their systems
Mechanisms to handle user complaints about generated content
Security filing with CAC for public-facing services

impact_assessment.detail: Generative AI services with public-facing products must complete a security assessment with the CAC before launch; assessment covers training data security and content safety.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits content that undermines national unity, threatens state power, harms social morality, or contains disinformation; effectively bans AI-generated content critical of the CCP or state.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual right to human review; platform-level editorial controls required.

private_right_of_action.detail: CAC and MIIT enforcement; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Requires consent for generating realistic depictions of real individuals; providers must implement content filtering and labeling for all AI-generated content.

biometric_data.detail: Processing biometric data for AI training requires explicit consent under PIPL framework as incorporated by reference.

training_data_transparency.detail: Training data must comply with Chinese content standards and data security laws; providers must document training data sources and pass security review.

content_labeling.detail: All AI-generated content must be labeled with visible or embedded markers; applies to images, audio, video, and text in public-facing products.

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination provisions; content restrictions focus on political and social stability.

risk_classification.detail: Services with public opinion influence or national security implications face heightened requirements; security assessment is the gatekeeping mechanism.

enforcement_model.detail: CAC/MIIT enforcement; service suspension, fines up to ¥500,000 (≈$70K); criminal referral for serious violations.

background.origin: Directly triggered by the global release of ChatGPT (November 2022) and rapid Chinese adoption; CAC was concerned about generative AI enabling creation of fake news, illegal content, and political dissent, as well as IP infringement and data security risks from training on Chinese personal data.
key_advocates: State Council's push for managed AI innovation
Chinese AI companies seeking regulatory clarity for their own legal risk
key_opposition: Chinese AI companies (Baidu, ByteDance, Alibaba Cloud) sought broader safe harbour provisions and less prescriptive content rules
unique_features: First national binding generative AI regulation globally — predated EU GPAI rules by two years
Content compliance obligation: generated content must not violate 'core socialist values' — politically unique globally
Security assessment requirement for GPAI services before public launch — creates pre-market approval mechanism
Data sourcing obligations: must comply with IP and personal data rules in training data collection
Algorithmic security assessment filings required with CAC
Applies to both domestic and foreign services accessible in China
background.legislative_notes: Draft circulated April 2023; public comment period May 2023; finalised July 10, 2023; effective August 15, 2023. Interim designation reflects that final permanent rules were deferred. Enforced through CAC's security assessment process — as of 2025 over 40 GPAI services have received CAC approval, including all major Chinese LLMs.

operative_dates: Effective 15 Aug 2023. Security assessment requirement for generative AI services with public opinion or social mobilisation capacity applies from same date.

full_name: Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis Internet Information Services
enforcement_body: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology
max_penalty: Up to RMB 50M or 5% annual turnover for serious violations
preemption_notes: National regulation issued by CAC, MIIT, and MPS jointly; sub-national implementation rules may supplement but cannot contradict this regulation.
summary: Regulates deep synthesis (deepfake/AI-generated) technology for video, voice, images, and text. Service providers must register users, implement ethics reviews, monitor content for illegal/disinformation use, and add visible labels to all synthetic content. Prohibits deepfakes implicating national security or reputational harm.
legal_citation: Provisions on the Management of Deep Synthesis Internet Information Services, CAC/MPS Order No. 11 (2022, eff. Jan. 10, 2023)
key_obligations: Providers must obtain consent before using individual likeness or voice for deep synthesis
Label AI-generated or significantly altered content with visible and non-visible markers
Security assessment and algorithm filing for public deep synthesis services
No creation of false news or content harmful to national security using deep synthesis

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed separately; CAC security assessment framework applies.

prohibited_categories.detail: Deep synthesis technologies may not be used to create content that undermines national unity, spreads disinformation, or disrupts social order.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: State enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: Requires explicit consent from depicted individuals for any realistic synthetic media involving their voice, image, or likeness; applies to all persons, not just public figures.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data used in deep synthesis must comply with PIPL consent requirements; providers must obtain explicit consent.

content_labeling.detail: All deep synthesis content must carry a prominent label; service providers must implement technical measures to mark AI-generated content.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed separately; covered by broader security tier framework.

enforcement_model.detail: CAC enforcement; service suspension and fines for violations.

full_name: Measures for Labelling of Artificial Intelligence-Generated Synthetic Content; Technical Standard GB45438-2025
max_penalty: Penalties under broader CAC cybersecurity frameworks
summary: Mandates visible and embedded (metadata/watermark) labels for all AI-generated and synthetic content distributed publicly in China, covering text, images, audio, video, and virtual scenes. Technical standard GB45438-2025 specifies metadata fields including provider code, content ID, and timestamp. Labels must persist when content is downloaded.
notable: Most technically specific AI watermarking standard globally. Preceded EU AI Act watermarking provisions.
legal_citation: GB 45438-2025 (AI-Generated Content Labelling Standard), SAMR/CAC (2025)
key_obligations: Standardised technical requirements for labelling AI-generated content
Explicit and implicit labelling methods specified
Applies to text, images, audio, and video AI-generated content
Platforms must implement labeling infrastructure meeting GB 45438 specifications

impact_assessment.detail: National standard; no impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: State enforcement; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Technical standard for labeling AI-generated content; all AI content must carry compliant labels per GB/T 45438 specification.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: National standard GB/T 45438 defines technical requirements for AI content labeling across all AI-generated media types; both visible and hidden labels required.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Enforcement by MIIT and CAC; non-compliant products may be withdrawn from market.

full_name: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China — AI-Relevant Provisions
max_penalty: RMB 50M (~$6.9M) or 5% annual turnover
summary: China's comprehensive personal data law directly applicable to AI: requires lawful basis for processing personal data in AI training, mandates consent for sensitive data, grants individuals rights to access, correct, and delete data, and prohibits differential treatment based on personal information analysis. AI recommendation algorithms must provide opt-out mechanisms.
legal_citation: Personal Information Protection Law of the People's Republic of China, Order No. 91 of the President (2021)
key_obligations: Individuals have right to explanation of automated decision-making affecting them
Right to refuse to be subject to automated decisions in commercial marketing and credit
Explicit consent for processing sensitive personal information
Data localization requirements for critical personal information handlers

impact_assessment.detail: Personal information protection impact assessments (PIPIAs) are mandatory for automated decision-making and sensitive personal information processing; must be filed with the CAC.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI categories; consent and processing restrictions apply.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 24 requires automated decisions affecting individuals to offer the right to explanation and human review; persons may refuse purely automated decisions in significant matters.

private_right_of_action.detail: Data subjects may file civil lawsuits for damages from PIPL violations; burden of proof shifted to processor once harm is shown.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is sensitive personal information requiring separate explicit consent, purpose limitation, and necessity analysis; strict cross-border transfer restrictions apply.

training_data_transparency.detail: Not specifically addressed; general data minimization principle applies.

anti_discrimination.detail: Art. 24 prohibits using personal information to impose unreasonable differential treatment; enforcement is weak compared to EU GDPR.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: CAC enforcement up to ¥50M or 5% annual revenue; individual liability for responsible persons up to ¥1M; civil actions available.

background.origin: Enacted as part of China's three-pillar digital legal framework alongside the Data Security Law (2021) and Cybersecurity Law (2017). Prompted by public backlash over data misuse by major platforms (Didi, Alibaba, ByteDance) and international pressure following GDPR, though consciously departing from GDPR's rights-based model.
key_drafters: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (NPC)
National Information Security Standardisation Technical Committee (TC260)
key_advocates: Consumer rights groups (exposure of platform data abuses)
State Council priorities on data sovereignty
Academic jurists from Renmin University and Peking University law schools
key_opposition: Domestic platform companies (Tencent, Alibaba, ByteDance) — implementation burden
Foreign multinationals concerned about cross-border transfer restrictions
unique_features: Extraterritorial reach broader than GDPR: applies to overseas processors of Chinese persons' data
Automated decision-making transparency right including right to refuse solely automated decisions
Legitimate interest basis narrower than GDPR — state security carve-outs explicit
Platform economy focus: separate obligations for large internet platforms
background.legislative_notes: Draft circulated August 2020; revised draft October 2021; enacted November 2021 with effect from November 1, 2021. Rapid passage through NPC compared to multi-year Western equivalents. CAC issued implementing regulations through 2022–2024.

full_name: Cybersecurity Technology — Generative AI Training Data Security Standards (Three-Part)
max_penalty: Enforcement through sectoral regulations
summary: Three national standards establish security requirements for GenAI training data: annotation security procedures, pre-training and fine-tuning data requirements, and basic service security standards. Mandate minimal use of 'unsafe' data, require regular model testing, and specify data provenance documentation.
legal_citation: GB/T 45694-2025 (Generative AI Training Data Standard), SAMR/MIIT (2025)
key_obligations: Technical requirements for training data quality assessment
Documentation requirements for dataset composition and annotation
Data provenance and lineage tracking for training datasets
Prohibited content categories in training data

impact_assessment.detail: Quality standards; no impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: State enforcement; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

training_data_transparency.detail: National standards for AI training data quality, labeling formats, and data governance documentation; does not require public disclosure.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Technical standards; voluntary for commercial entities unless incorporated by reference into mandatory regulations.

full_name: Online Safety Act 2023
max_penalty: £18M or 10% qualifying worldwide revenue
preemption_notes: UK sovereign law post-Brexit; Ofcom regulatory guidance supplements the Act. No supranational preemption risk post-Brexit.
summary: UK Online Safety Act imposes platform duties to prevent illegal content, protect children, and ensure user safety. AI chatbots and generative AI systems are in scope as of Ofcom guidance from 2026. Requires risk assessments, proactive content moderation technology, and Ofcom registration for regulated services. UK has no dedicated AI Act.
notable: UK's primary binding AI-relevant instrument; UK government explicitly rejected standalone AI Act in favour of sector-specific principles-based approach.
legal_citation: Online Safety Act 2023, c. 50 (UK)
key_obligations: Platforms must proactively assess and mitigate AI-generated harmful content risks
Criminal offence to share non-consensual intimate deepfake images
Category 1 services must conduct annual transparency reports on AI content moderation
Ofcom to produce codes of practice for AI content harms
Age verification requirements for platforms with AI-generated adult content

impact_assessment.detail: Platforms must conduct risk assessments to identify illegal and harmful content before launching or significantly changing AI-driven recommendation systems; ongoing safety duties.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not prohibit AI uses directly; imposes platform duties to prevent specified categories of illegal content.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed for individuals; platforms must implement human review processes for content moderation.

private_right_of_action.detail: Ofcom enforcement only; no private right of action against platforms.

synthetic_media.detail: Platforms must implement systems to detect, remove, and prevent sharing of AI-generated NCII (non-consensual intimate images); criminal offense for sharing deepfake sexual content.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed specifically.

risk_classification.detail: Platform risk assessment duties based on size and content type; no AI system risk classification.

enforcement_model.detail: Ofcom may impose fines up to £18M or 10% of global annual turnover; criminal liability for senior managers of non-compliant platforms.

background.origin: Online Safety Act emerged from the Online Harms White Paper (2019) and was dramatically reshaped by the death of 14-year-old Molly Russell (2017, inquest 2022), whose Instagram and Pinterest feeds had contained self-harm content, establishing the harm-to-children case for the legislation.
key_drafters: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT)
Ian Russell (Molly's father, named in parliamentary tributes as key influence)
Lord John Moylan (House of Lords rapporteur)
key_opposition: Meta, Apple, WhatsApp, Signal (encryption provisions)
Index on Censorship, Open Rights Group (free expression concerns)
Journalists and press freedom groups (legal but harmful content)
Cross-party concerns over encrypted messaging scanning
unique_features: Client-side scanning provisions — uniquely controversial globally
Safety-by-design obligation from the product development stage
Super-complaints mechanism for civil society organisations
Adult content verification requirements on porn platforms — globally rare
background.legislative_notes: White Paper April 2019; draft Online Safety Bill introduced May 2021; substantially revised twice (Secretary of State powers removed in 2022); passed October 2023. Encryption provisions suspended pending "accredited technology" announcement from Ofcom. Ofcom began phased enforcement codes 2024.

operative_dates: Royal Assent: Oct 2023. Illegal harms duties: Mar 2024. Children's safety codes: Jan 2025. Transparency reporting: 2025–2026 (staggered by platform size).

full_name: Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust
max_penalty: KRW 30M (~$21,000) per violation
preemption_notes: National framework law; sector-specific ministries issue subordinate regulations that must align with this act. Local governments may not enact conflicting AI rules.
summary: South Korea's comprehensive AI framework consolidates 19 bills, requiring developers and deployers of 'high-impact AI' (healthcare, finance, transportation, employment) to meet transparency and safety obligations. Mandates AI use disclosure to users. Low penalties reflect innovation-first design; 1-year enforcement grace period means effective enforcement begins January 2027.
notable: Passed December 2024, effective January 2026. Innovation-first design with light penalties contrasts with EU approach.
legal_citation: Act on Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of Trust (AI Basic Act), Act No. 20882 (2024)
key_obligations: Government to establish national AI basic plan every 3 years
High-impact AI systems subject to conformity assessment
Providers of high-impact AI must disclose information to users
AI providers must implement measures to prevent discriminatory outcomes
National AI Commission to coordinate AI governance across ministries

impact_assessment.detail: High-impact AI systems must undergo safety review through the AI Safety Research Institute; government AI systems face additional impact assessments before deployment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Framework law; specific prohibitions delegated to sector-specific regulations.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals affected by high-impact AI decisions have the right to request explanation and review; deployers must provide accessible redress.

private_right_of_action.detail: Government enforcement; no private right of action in the basic act.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed in the basic act; addressed in separate deepfake-specific laws.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed; covered by PIPA and other sectoral laws.

anti_discrimination.detail: Basic act requires AI to respect human dignity and equality; substantive anti-discrimination deferred to existing civil rights framework.

risk_classification.detail: Classifies AI into high-impact and general categories based on use context; framework act delegates binding product obligations to sector-specific rules.

enforcement_model.detail: MSIT oversight; civil penalties for high-impact AI violations; criminal liability for specific offenses.

background.origin: Driven by South Korea's National AI Strategy (2019) and the Presidential Committee on the Fourth Industrial Revolution; accelerated by ChatGPT's emergence in 2022 and the international AI governance race following the EU AI Act; strong interest from MSICT in positioning Korea as a global AI leader with its own regulatory model.
key_drafters: National Assembly Science and Technology Committee
Korea Institute for Information Security and Cryptology (technical input)
key_advocates: Major Korean tech companies (Samsung, Kakao, Naver) who preferred Korean regulation to extraterritorial EU AI Act
key_opposition: Some civil society groups concerned the law was too weak on prohibited practices and enforcement
Labour unions worried about insufficient employment AI protections
unique_features: Second-enacted national comprehensive AI law globally (after the EU AI Act)
Applies blanket transparency obligations regardless of the system's position in the AI value chain (unlike EU's deployer-heavy model)
Mandatory labeling of all generative AI outputs — broader than EU requirement
Establishes AI Safety Research Institute as permanent government body
Foreign operator representative requirement — Korean residents must have a local representative for extraterritorial enforcement
Public support provisions: government subsidies, AI competitiveness fund, and mandatory AI literacy education
background.legislative_notes: Multiple AI framework bills introduced in the 20th and 21st National Assemblies from 2020 onward; consolidated bill passed the National Assembly on January 9, 2025; promulgated January 22, 2025; transition period expired January 22, 2026 when full obligations came into force.

implementation_phases.description: South Korea AI Basic Act enacted
Act takes effect (13 months after enactment)
High-impact AI obligations and registration requirements fully apply

operative_dates: Enacted Jan 2025; enters into force Jan 2026 (one-year implementation period). High-impact AI designation rules to be issued by Minister within 6 months of entry into force.

full_name: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 — Automated Decision-Making Provisions
enforcement_body: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
max_penalty: AUD 62,600 per violation
preemption_notes: Federal law with concurrent state/territory application. Commonwealth law prevails over inconsistent state law under s.109 of the Constitution. State equivalents exist in some jurisdictions.
summary: Amends Australia's Privacy Act to require APP entities to disclose automated decision-making processes in privacy policies where AI could significantly affect individual rights or interests. Transparency obligation only — no prohibition or assessment requirement. Effective December 2026.
notable: Australia rejected mandatory AI guardrails in December 2025 in favour of voluntary guidance. This privacy amendment is Australia's only binding AI-specific obligation.
legal_citation: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (Cth) (Automated Decision-Making Amendments)
key_obligations: Organizations using ADM for decisions significantly affecting individuals must update privacy policies to disclose
Right to seek explanation of ADM decisions affecting individuals
Mandatory privacy impact assessments for high-privacy-risk activities including ADM
OAIC to develop guidance on ADM transparency requirements

impact_assessment.detail: Privacy Impact Assessments required for high-privacy-risk activities including AI systems processing sensitive information; OAIC may require PIAs for any high-risk processing.

prohibited_categories.detail: Privacy law; does not prohibit AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have the right to know about automated decision-making affecting them and receive an explanation; no right to refuse automated decisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: New direct right of action for serious privacy invasions; OAIC can bring representative complaints; courts may award damages including non-economic loss.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed specifically in the Privacy Act amendments.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data remains sensitive information requiring consent; enhanced security safeguards under 2024 amendments.

anti_discrimination.detail: Privacy Act prohibits use of personal information for discriminatory profiling; defers to Racial Discrimination Act and similar for substantive standard.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: OAIC civil penalties up to A$50M for serious and repeated violations; new private action pathway through Federal Court.

background.origin: The Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 implemented the first tranche of reforms from the Attorney-General's Department review of the Privacy Act 1988 (completed 2022). The review was triggered by the Optus (2022) and Medibank (2022) data breaches affecting millions of Australians.
key_drafters: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security (review role)
Gilbert + Tobin (legal consultant to the review)
key_opposition: Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) on compliance costs
Media industry on journalism exemption narrowing
Adtech industry on data broker provisions
unique_features: Introduces a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy — first in Australia
Dovetail mechanism aligning Privacy Act with Online Safety Act enforcement
Automated decision-making transparency requirement for significant decisions — Australia's first ADM-specific obligation
Strengthened children's online privacy protections (online privacy code pathway)
background.legislative_notes: Privacy Act Review Report published February 2023 (116 recommendations). Government response October 2023 (supported majority). Amendment Act introduced 2024; passed with bipartisan support. Second tranche of reforms (right to erasure, direct action) to follow in separate legislation.

full_name: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and Rule of Law
enforcement_body: Committee of Parties (upon entry into force)
max_penalty: Varies by ratifying state
preemption_notes: Binding upon ratification; not yet in force (requires 5 ratifications including 3 CoE members)
summary: First binding international AI treaty, opened for signature September 2024. Requires signatory states to ensure AI systems respect human rights, democratic principles, and rule of law. Mandates impact assessments, transparency, accountability, and remedies. 37 signatories as of April 2026; no ratifications yet — not yet in force.
notable: Binding upon ratification but not yet in force. 37 signatories include EU, US, Canada, UK, Japan, Israel, Uruguay. Entry into force requires 5 ratifications (minimum 3 Council of Europe members).
legal_citation: Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law, CETS No. 225 (2024)
key_obligations: Parties must ensure AI lifecycle activities respect human rights
Prohibition on AI that undermines integrity of democratic institutions
Right to seek review of AI-assisted decisions by public authorities
Parties must establish independent oversight bodies for AI
Transparency obligations for AI systems used by or on behalf of public authorities

impact_assessment.detail: Parties must assess risks and potential impacts of AI systems on human rights, democracy, and rule of law before and during deployment; assessment obligations are binding on government use.

prohibited_categories.detail: Framework convention; specific prohibitions delegated to domestic implementation.

human_review_rights.detail: Parties must ensure individuals can seek review of AI decisions affecting their rights; effective remedy and redress mechanisms required.

private_right_of_action.detail: Treaty obligations on state parties; domestic implementation determines individual remedies.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed specifically; covered under general fundamental rights protections.

anti_discrimination.detail: Parties must assess AI impacts on non-discrimination rights; obligations draw on the European Convention on Human Rights framework.

risk_classification.detail: Framework convention establishing principles; delegates risk classification to domestic law; first binding international AI treaty.

enforcement_model.detail: Conference of Parties (COP) oversight; compliance through domestic legal implementation; no supranational enforcement body.

background.origin: Council of Europe AI treaty process began in 2019 through the Ad hoc Committee on Artificial Intelligence (CAHAI), driven by member states' concern that AI posed risks to human rights, democracy, and the rule of law not addressed by existing conventions. The Framework Convention draws on the ECHR and existing CoE instruments.
key_drafters: Committee on Artificial Intelligence (CAI, successor to CAHAI)
key_advocates: Civil society organisations at CoE (Access Now, Amnesty)
key_opposition: Some signatories (US, UK, Israel) pushed for non-binding interpretive annexes to accommodate private sector flexibility
Industry groups sought narrower scope for private sector obligations
unique_features: First international treaty on AI — binding under international law on ratifying states
Applies to both public AND private sector AI systems (with flexibility for private sector implementation mode)
Explicitly links AI governance to the European Convention on Human Rights
Open to non-Council of Europe states — US, UK, Israel, Canada, Japan, and others signed
Requires parties to establish remedies for AI-caused human rights violations
Creates follow-up mechanism (Conference of Parties) to monitor implementation
background.legislative_notes: CAHAI established 2019; work transferred to CAI 2022; final text adopted by Committee of Ministers May 17, 2024; opened for signature September 5, 2024; first signatures at ceremony in Vilnius September 5, 2024 (EU, US, UK, Israel, Norway, Andorra, Georgia, Iceland, San Marino, Moldova). Not yet in force — requires 5 ratifications.

full_name: Act on Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-Related Technologies
enforcement_body: Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications
max_penalty: No direct monetary penalties; enforcement via guidance and sector-specific law
preemption_notes: National law; no sub-national preemption dynamic in Japan for this type of framework legislation. Prefecture-level AI guidelines exist but are subordinate to national law.
summary: Japan's first binding AI law establishes a national AI promotion framework with cabinet-level AI Strategy Headquarters. Emphasizes research investment, talent development, and international AI leadership rather than restrictions. No direct monetary penalties — relies on sector-specific laws and guidance for enforcement. Deliberate contrast to EU's risk-based prohibitive approach.
notable: Innovation-first framework law. Represents Japan's 'soft law' approach to AI governance.
legal_citation: Act for the Promotion of Research, Development and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence-related Technologies, Act No. 14 of 2025 (Japan)
key_obligations: Government to develop basic AI policy and implementation guidelines
Establish AI Safety Institute with authority to conduct safety evaluations
Promote AI development while ensuring human-centric safety principles
Develop technical standards for AI safety assessment in consultation with international bodies

impact_assessment.detail: Developers of foundation AI models must implement safety evaluation processes aligned with the Hiroshima AI Process principles; government provides guidelines for risk assessment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Promotion-oriented framework; no prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed in this act.

private_right_of_action.detail: Not addressed.

synthetic_media.detail: Addressed separately in intellectual property guidelines.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed in this act.

risk_classification.detail: Establishes national AI promotion framework with basic principles; safety and reliability obligations delegated to sector-specific guidelines rather than binding product rules.

enforcement_model.detail: Primarily enabling legislation; enforcement mechanisms delegated to sector-specific agencies.

background.origin: Emerged from Japan's 2022 AI Strategy and growing international pressure to establish a legal AI governance framework following the EU AI Act and G7 Hiroshima Process (which Japan chaired in 2023). The law was designed to be enabling rather than restrictive, reflecting Japan's concern about falling behind in AI capability.
key_drafters: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
Expert panel chaired by Professor Hiroshi Nakagawa
key_opposition: Consumer groups concerned about lack of binding obligations
Opposition parties (CDP) pushing for stronger enforcement
Civil society groups on surveillance AI and bias
unique_features: Promotional framing rather than risk-based: government obligations to support AI development
Sector-specific guidelines issued by individual ministries rather than unified rules
International cooperation mandate reflecting G7 and OECD AI Principles commitment
Human dignity and fundamental rights provisions weaker than EU counterpart
background.legislative_notes: Policy discussion papers from 2022; expert council recommendations 2024; Diet debate and passage early 2025. Japan deliberately timed the law to align with Expo 2025 Osaka, which featured AI prominently. Law creates framework for future binding regulations through cabinet orders.

full_name: California Consumer Privacy Act / California Privacy Rights Act — Automated Decision-Making Technology Regulations
max_penalty: $2,500 per unintentional violation; $7,500 per intentional violation
summary: CCPA/CPRA grants Californians rights to opt out of automated decision-making technology (ADMT), request human review of significant AI decisions, and access data used in profiling. CPRA's 2023 ADMT regulations required by CPPA are among the most expansive in the US for limiting algorithmic profiling.
notable: CPPA's ADMT regulations (effective 2023) added human review rights and opt-out from profiling — one of the most expansive US AI individual rights provisions.
key_obligations: Right to opt out of automated decision-making using sensitive personal information
Right to know when profiling is used to make consequential decisions
Right to limit use of sensitive personal information in AI systems
CPPA to issue regulations on automated decision-making technology access and correction rights

impact_assessment.detail: CCPA/CPRA does not mandate AI-specific impact assessments; risk assessments are required by CPRA for certain data processing but not specific to AI.

prohibited_categories.detail: No AI-specific prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Consumers have the right to know about automated decision-making that significantly affects them; CPRA requires explanation of automated decisions but stops short of a right to opt out.

private_right_of_action.detail: Limited to data breach context ($100–$750 statutory damages); general privacy violations enforced by AG/CPPA only.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is a "sensitive personal information" category under CPRA; consumers may opt out of its sale/sharing.

training_data_transparency.detail: No specific training data disclosure; general data collection notice requirements apply.

anti_discrimination.detail: Non-discrimination right prohibits using CCPA rights exercise against consumers; does not create independent AI anti-discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: CPPA/AG enforcement up to $7,500 per intentional violation; limited private right for data breaches.

background.origin: The California Consumer Privacy Act emerged from Alistair Mactaggart's personal interest in consumer privacy after conversations with a Google engineer friend revealed the scope of data collection. Mactaggart, a real estate developer, personally funded a ballot initiative effort with over $3 million. Facing the prospect of an inflexible ballot measure, the California legislature passed a negotiated compromise statute in June 2018 — nine days before the ballot initiative deadline — with Mactaggart withdrawing his initiative in exchange for a legislative vehicle. The AI-specific provisions were expanded substantially by CPRA (Prop 24, 2020) and subsequent CPPA rulemaking.
key_drafters: California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) staff (CPRA rulemaking)
key_advocates: Californians for Consumer Privacy (Mactaggart's ballot initiative org)
key_opposition: California Chamber of Commerce
TechNet
Google
Facebook
Amazon
Microsoft
Association of National Advertisers
unique_features: Only major US privacy law originating from a ballot initiative threat rather than legislative process
Created the California Privacy Protection Agency — the first dedicated state-level privacy regulator in the US
Opt-out right for sale/sharing of personal information, including in AI training contexts
Regulations on automated decision-making technology (ADMT) issued by CPPA are the most granular US ADM rules at any level
background.legislative_notes: CCPA enacted June 28, 2018, effective January 1, 2020. CPRA (Proposition 24) passed November 3, 2020 (56% yes), effective January 1, 2023. CPPA's ADMT regulations (covering high-risk automated decision-making) went through multiple notice-and-comment rounds from 2022-2025. Final ADMT rules are expected in 2025-2026 and will substantially expand California's reach over AI systems.

full_name: Responsible AI Safety and Education Act
enforcement_body: New York Department of Financial Services
max_penalty: Civil penalty: $1,000 per employee per violation; $10,000 willful violations
summary: New York's frontier AI safety law requires large AI developers to establish and publish safety protocols, report critical incidents to the state within 72 hours, and maintain documented safety practices. Applies to frontier models developed, deployed, or operating in New York. Creates a new state AI oversight office within DFS.
notable: Chapter amendment signed March 27, 2026. New York's answer to California SB 53.
legal_citation: N.Y. Lab. Law §§ 193-aa to 193-ff (RAISE Act); S 3511-A / A 4736-A, 2025
key_obligations: Employers must notify workers before deploying high-risk AI in employment decisions
Conduct algorithmic impact assessments annually
Workers may request explanation of AI decision affecting them
Right to request human review of high-risk AI employment decision
Independent audit required for high-risk AI used in employment

impact_assessment.detail: Employers using AI in high-stakes employment decisions must conduct annual third-party bias audits and publicly disclose results.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI uses; focuses on audit and transparency.

human_review_rights.detail: No right to human review specified.

private_right_of_action.detail: State enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

anti_discrimination.detail: Requires bias audit publication; similar to NYC LL 144 but with broader scope covering assessment, screening, and monitoring tools.

risk_classification.detail: Employment sector only; no general risk classification.

enforcement_model.detail: Civil penalties enforced by NY AG; modest per-violation amounts.

full_name: AI Governance Framework and Election Integrity Act
max_penalty: No standalone civil penalty; AG enforcement through consumer protection remedies
summary: Establishes AI governance for Kentucky state government with risk-based oversight by Commonwealth Office of Technology. Requires AI inventory and pre-implementation approval for consequential government AI systems. Adds election integrity provisions requiring disclosure of AI-generated political content.
notable: Passed 30-3 in Senate, 86-10 in House. Primary scope is state government AI use, not private sector.
legal_citation: KRS § 42.740 et seq. (AI Governance Framework); SB 4, 2025 Ky. Gen. Assem.
key_obligations: Establishes AI governance framework for state government AI use
State agencies must inventory and assess AI systems for risk
Requires AI policies for high-risk government AI deployment
Creates AI advisory body within state government

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Not addressed.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: AI chatbots must disclose AI nature to Kentucky consumers upon sincere request.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: AG enforcement; civil penalties.

full_name: Connecticut Data Privacy Act Amendment — LLM Training Data Disclosure
max_penalty: Civil penalty: up to $25,000 per violation per day
summary: Amends Connecticut Data Privacy Act to require controllers to disclose in privacy notices whether they collect, use, or sell personal data to train large language models. First US state law making LLM training data use a mandatory privacy disclosure element.
notable: First state requiring explicit LLM training data disclosure in privacy notices, not just general AI data use.
legal_citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. § 42-600a et seq.; PA 25-113, 2025 Conn. Gen. Assem.
key_obligations: LLM developers above compute threshold must publish training data summary
Disclosure must include categories of training data, sources, and whether copyrighted material was used
Content generated by covered LLMs must be labeled as AI-generated

impact_assessment.detail: Developers and deployers of high-risk AI must conduct impact assessments before deployment and annually thereafter; must address copyright and intellectual property provenance.

prohibited_categories.detail: Risk-based obligations; no specific prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Consumers may request human review of consequential AI decisions; deployers must provide meaningful recourse.

private_right_of_action.detail: AG enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed specifically.

training_data_transparency.detail: Impact assessments must address copyright and intellectual property provenance of training data; developers must document data sourcing and licensing.

anti_discrimination.detail: Deployers must use reasonable care to prevent algorithmic discrimination; impact-based standard.

risk_classification.detail: Applies to high-risk AI making consequential decisions in specified domains.

enforcement_model.detail: AG civil enforcement; penalties per violation.

full_name: New Hampshire AI Chatbot Child Harm Prevention Act
max_penalty: $1,000 per violation (private action); 90-day cure before AG enforcement
summary: Prohibits AI chatbot operators from facilitating or encouraging harmful conduct toward children, including sexual exploitation, illegal drug use, self-harm, and violence. Provides private right of action for minors and parents with $1,000 statutory damages. AG enforcement available after 90-day cure notice.
legal_citation: RSA § 358-A:10-d; HB 143, 2025 N.H. Gen. Court
key_obligations: Chatbot operators must disclose AI identity to users under 18
Criminal prohibition on AI-generated CSAM
Crisis protocol required when minors express suicidal ideation to chatbot
AG enforcement

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: AI chatbots must disclose their AI nature to NH consumers upon sincere inquiry.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

full_name: Act to Ensure Transparency in Consumer Transactions Involving Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: $100–$1,000 per incident; civil consumer damages
summary: Prohibits AI chatbots from misleading consumers into believing they are interacting with a human without clear conspicuous notice. Violations treated as Unfair Trade Practices Act violations. Separate from LD 2082, which covers mental health specifically.
notable: Distinct from Maine LD 2082 (AI therapy prohibition). HP 1154 is a general chatbot identity disclosure requirement.
legal_citation: Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 10, § 1445 et seq.; HP 1154 / LD 1547, 132nd Me. Leg.
key_obligations: Chatbot operators must disclose AI identity when sincerely asked
Prohibition on claiming to be human when sincerely questioned
AG enforcement; civil penalties per violation

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.
