biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: AI systems engaging with Maine consumers must identify themselves as AI when asked.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: AG enforcement; civil penalties.

full_name: Mental Health Chatbots Consumer Protection Act
max_penalty: Civil penalty: up to $2,500 per violation by AG
summary: Requires mental health chatbots — AI that simulates licensed mental health professional conversations — to disclose their AI nature at multiple touchpoints: before access, if 7+ days since last use, and when asked by user. Applies to apps and platforms that simulate confidential therapy conversations.
legal_citation: Utah Code Ann. § 13-72-501; HB 452, 2024 Utah Gen. Sess.
key_obligations: Mental health chatbots must disclose AI identity clearly
Must provide access to licensed professional resources
Cannot represent as licensed mental health provider

full_name: Montana Right to Compute Act
max_penalty: No private right of action; declaratory relief only
summary: Establishes a fundamental right to privately own and use computational resources in Montana. Any government restriction on computing resources must be narrowly tailored and demonstrably necessary. Requires AI-controlled critical infrastructure operators to develop NIST-based risk management policies and annual safety reviews.
notable: First-in-nation law establishing a right to compute. Primarily protects individuals and businesses from government restrictions on AI/compute use.
legal_citation: Mont. Code Ann. § 2-17-601 et seq.; SB 212, 2025 Mont. Leg.
key_obligations: Government agencies prohibited from using AI to deny individual rights based on protected class
Residents have right to access and operate AI computing without government interference
Prohibition on social credit scoring by government entities

full_name: Michigan Public Acts 263-266 — AI in Political Advertising Package
max_penalty: Class E felony — up to 5 years imprisonment (HB 5145)
summary: Four-bill package criminalizing AI-generated deepfakes in elections. Requires disclosure of AI use in political ads. Criminalizes knowingly distributing materially deceptive AI media within 90 days of election with intent to harm a candidate or deceive voters. Establishes Class E felony penalties. One of the earliest state election deepfake laws.
key_obligations: Prohibition on creating or distributing deepfake political ads without disclosure
Criminal prohibition on materially deceptive synthetic media about candidates
Disclosure required on AI-generated election communications
AG and election officials may seek injunctive relief

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: PA 266 provides civil remedy for depicted individuals.

synthetic_media.detail: PA 263 criminalizes election-related deepfakes (4-year felony); PA 266 provides civil remedy for all AI-generated NCII, not just election context.

full_name: Washington Forged Digital Likeness Act
max_penalty: $3,000 per civil violation; gross misdemeanor (criminal)
summary: Broadly criminalizes forged digital likenesses — AI-manipulated audio or video indistinguishable from genuine and likely to deceive. Applies to creation and distribution. Provides both criminal (gross misdemeanor) and civil ($3,000/violation) remedies. Carve-outs for satire, public interest, and fair use.
legal_citation: RCW §§ 63.60.010 et seq. (as amended); HB 1205, 2025 Wash. Leg.
key_obligations: Extends Washington right of publicity to cover digital replicas and AI-generated likenesses
Consent required for commercial use of digital replica
Prohibition on non-consensual AI replicas for sexual content
Civil action: actual damages plus up to $10,000 per violation

impact_assessment.detail: Requires developers and deployers of high-risk AI in employment contexts to conduct pre-deployment assessments for discriminatory effects.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Workers and job applicants subject to AI-assisted decisions may request human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: AG enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

anti_discrimination.detail: Employers must use reasonable care to prevent AI from producing discriminatory employment outcomes; impact-based standard.

risk_classification.detail: Employment sector only.

enforcement_model.detail: AG civil enforcement; penalties per violation.

full_name: Law on Artificial Intelligence No. 134/2025/QH15
max_penalty: Administrative sanctions; enforcement details in implementing regulations
preemption_notes: National law; Vietnam is a unitary state. Provincial authorities implement but cannot contradict national AI law. Ministry of Science and Technology holds primary regulatory authority.
summary: Vietnam's first standalone comprehensive AI law establishes risk-based classification (high, medium, low risk) for AI systems. High-risk applications in finance, healthcare, and education have an 18-month grace period (until September 2027); other sectors have 12 months. Applies to both domestic and foreign AI providers affecting Vietnam.
notable: One of the first comprehensive AI laws in Southeast Asia. Risk-based framework modelled on EU AI Act.
legal_citation: Law No. 134/2025/QH15 on Artificial Intelligence (Vietnam)
key_obligations: AI developers and deployers of high-risk AI must register with competent authorities
High-risk AI must undergo conformity assessment
AI systems must meet safety and reliability standards set by Ministry of Science and Technology
Foreign AI service providers must comply with data localization requirements

impact_assessment.detail: High-risk AI systems must undergo safety evaluation by certified bodies before deployment; sectoral authorities conduct evaluations for their regulated domains.

prohibited_categories.detail: Risk-based approach; no explicit prohibited categories though national security content restrictions apply.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals may request explanation and review of consequential AI decisions; deployers must provide accessible redress mechanisms.

private_right_of_action.detail: Government enforcement; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Not specifically addressed in the AI law; cybersecurity law provisions apply.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data requires explicit consent and purpose limitation; data localization requirements apply.

content_labeling.detail: Not addressed in the AI law.

risk_classification.detail: AI systems classified as high-risk in designated sectors (healthcare, education, banking, critical infrastructure) face enhanced obligations; binary classification with binding requirements.

enforcement_model.detail: BKHCN enforcement; civil and administrative penalties; criminal liability for intentional serious violations.

background.origin: Part of Vietnam's broader digital transformation agenda under Resolution 52 (2019) and the Digital Economy Strategy. Prompted by rapid AI adoption in Vietnamese industry (banking, manufacturing) and concerns about Chinese AI platform dominance. Vietnam drew heavily on the EU AI Act and South Korean Basic Act models.
key_drafters: Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology
key_advocates: Vietnam Software and IT Services Association (VINASA)
Vietnamese startups and AI research community
key_opposition: Foreign tech companies concerned about data localisation requirements
SMEs worried about compliance costs for high-risk AI classification
unique_features: First Southeast Asian nation with a comprehensive AI law
Mandatory AI liability insurance for high-risk applications — unique globally
State AI ethics committee with enforcement powers
Explicit provisions on AI in national defence and security sector
background.legislative_notes: Draft law prepared 2023; public consultation 2024; National Assembly passed Law No. 134/2025 in early 2025. Came into force with implementation regulations to follow from MOST and sector ministries.

implementation_phases.description: Vietnam AI Law enacted
General transparency and disclosure obligations take effect
High-risk AI classification and assessment obligations apply
Mandatory AI liability insurance requirement takes effect

operative_dates: Effective 1 Jan 2026. AI system registration and conformity assessment obligations phased: critical AI systems 6 months post-enactment; general AI systems 18 months.

full_name: Thailand Artificial Intelligence Act
max_penalty: Administrative penalty: up to THB 2,000,000 (~$55,000) per violation; criminal sanctions for prohibited practices
preemption_notes: National law; Thailand is a unitary state. The Digital Economy and Society Ministry leads implementation; no sub-national AI law variation.
summary: Thailand's AI Act establishes a three-tier risk system: prohibited unacceptable-risk AI, high-risk systems requiring registration and risk management under ISO/IEC 42001:2023, and lower-risk systems with lighter obligations. High-risk providers must register, implement risk management, report serious incidents, and ensure human oversight.
notable: corpus boundary case — verify inclusion; official text URL not yet available in English. Details from TCCT implementation guidelines March 25, 2026.
legal_citation: Artificial Intelligence Act B.E. 2569 (2026) (Thailand)
key_obligations: High-risk AI operators must obtain certification from National AI Committee
AI developers must register AI systems with regulatory authority
Disclosure obligations for AI use in public-facing applications
Establish AI Supervisory Committee with cross-ministry membership

impact_assessment.detail: AI operators in high-risk categories must obtain prior authorization through safety evaluations conducted by the AI Regulatory Authority.

prohibited_categories.detail: Framework law; specific prohibitions in subordinate regulations.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals subject to high-risk AI decisions have the right to explanation and human review; operators must establish accessible complaint mechanisms.

private_right_of_action.detail: NEMA enforcement; no private right of action in the base law.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Covered by PDPA.

anti_discrimination.detail: AI Act requires non-discrimination in AI deployment; substantive standard deferred to existing Thai civil rights and consumer protection framework.

risk_classification.detail: NEMA classifies AI systems into high-risk and standard categories; high-risk requires prior authorization and ongoing monitoring.

enforcement_model.detail: NEMA enforcement; fines up to ฿10M for serious violations; suspension of AI service authorization for non-compliance.

background.origin: Thailand's AI Act emerged from NECTEC (National Electronics and Computer Technology Center) recommendations and a parliamentary committee review of the 2022 National AI Strategy. The Act was accelerated after Thailand observed Vietnam, Singapore, and other ASEAN peers advancing AI governance frameworks.
key_advocates: Thai Chamber of Commerce AI Working Group
key_opposition: SME associations concerned about high-risk classification burden
Healthcare sector resisting strict AI medical device rules
Civil society groups (iLaw) concerned about government AI surveillance exemptions
unique_features: Covers AI systems deployed in Thailand regardless of developer location — explicit extraterritorial reach
Mandatory national AI registry for high-risk systems
AI Ethics Board with power to issue binding guidelines — distinct from Western regulator models
Sector-specific sandboxes co-administered by ETDA and Bank of Thailand
background.legislative_notes: Preliminary draft released 2024; public consultation three rounds; National Assembly passed 2026. Phased implementation: prohibited practices and definitions immediately; high-risk obligations 18 months; GPAI obligations 24 months after enactment.

implementation_phases.description: Thailand AI Act enacted
General provisions and prohibited practices take effect
High-risk AI obligations fully apply (18 months after enactment)
GPAI model obligations apply (24 months after enactment)

full_name: Provisions on the Administration of Algorithmic Recommendations in Internet Information Services
enforcement_body: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology
max_penalty: Administrative fines; service suspension; criminal liability for serious violations
preemption_notes: National regulation issued by CAC; sub-national jurisdictions (Shanghai, Beijing) have issued additional implementation guidance that must remain consistent with this regulation.
summary: First globally binding regulation of algorithmic recommendation systems. Requires platforms with 1M+ users to register recommendation algorithms, offer non-personalized options, enable user preference modification, conduct risk assessments, and report to regulators. Prohibits discriminatory pricing and addictive design patterns targeting minors.
notable: Predates EU AI Act. Globally first binding algorithmic recommendation law. Prohibits 'big data price discrimination' — using algorithms to charge existing customers more than new users.
legal_citation: Provisions on the Management of Algorithmic Recommendations, CAC/MIIT/MPS/SAMR/MCC Order No. 9 (2022)
key_obligations: Users have right to opt out of personalised algorithmic recommendations
Prohibition on using algorithms to create addictive features for minors
Prohibition on price discrimination using personal characteristics
Gig economy platforms must explain how work allocation algorithms function
Large platforms must file algorithm registry with CAC

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits algorithmic recommendations that incite addiction, spread disinformation, undermine national unity, or push users toward illegal content or radicalization.

human_review_rights.detail: Users must be given the right to turn off personalized recommendations; providers must implement human editorial review for recommendation content.

private_right_of_action.detail: CAC enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: Algorithm recommendation services must label content as algorithmically recommended and disclose when AI is driving content selection.

anti_discrimination.detail: Anti-addiction provisions protect against exploitative targeting; no civil rights anti-discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: CAC enforcement; fines up to ¥100,000 and service suspension for violations.

background.origin: Emerged from CAC concern about algorithmic amplification of extremist content, commercial manipulation of users through dark patterns, price discrimination by ride-hailing and e-commerce platforms, and the social impact of dopamine-loop design in short video apps (Douyin/TikTok). Preceded by CAC's 2021 Guidelines on Internet Information Service Algorithms.
key_drafters: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT)
key_advocates: State Council policy emphasis on digital economy governance
Consumer rights complaints about algorithmic pricing discrimination
key_opposition: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent, and major platform operators sought narrower labeling and user right provisions
unique_features: First regulation globally to specifically govern algorithmic content recommendation systems at national scale
User right to opt out of personalised recommendation and switch to non-personalised feeds
Prohibition on algorithm-induced addiction, price discrimination, and 'hot topic' manipulation for commercial gain
Mandatory algorithm filing/registration with CAC — first government algorithm registry
Real-name registration requirement for major recommendation algorithm accounts
background.legislative_notes: Draft circulated August 2021; public consultation September 2021; finalised December 2021; entered force March 1, 2022. Enforced through CAC's regulatory actions against major platforms including ByteDance (Douyin algorithm audit) and Alibaba throughout 2022–2024.

short_name: India Digital Personal Data Protection Act
full_name: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
max_penalty: Up to Rs 250 crore (~$30M USD) for serious breaches
preemption_notes: Central (federal) law; state governments have no parallel data protection competence. DPDPA is directly applicable across all Indian states and union territories.
summary: India's first comprehensive data protection law with AI-relevant provisions covering automated processing and data subject rights for AI-processed personal data. Establishes the Data Protection Board of India for enforcement. Implementing rules still being finalized as of April 2026 — enforcement not yet fully active.
notable: Implementing rules not yet finalized as of April 2026. Full enforcement pending. AI-specific provisions are implicit rather than explicit.
legal_citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, No. 22 of 2023 (India)
key_obligations: Data fiduciaries must process personal data only with consent for specified purposes
Right to access information about personal data processing
Right to erasure of personal data
Data fiduciaries must implement reasonable security safeguards
Significant data fiduciaries (volume threshold) subject to additional obligations including data protection officer

impact_assessment.detail: Significant data fiduciaries must conduct Data Protection Impact Assessments; DPDPB may mandate DPIAs for high-risk AI processing contexts.

prohibited_categories.detail: Privacy law; does not prohibit AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Data principals have the right to grievance redress and to challenge automated decisions; fiduciaries must establish accessible complaint mechanisms.

private_right_of_action.detail: DPDPB enforcement only; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data requires explicit consent; significant data fiduciaries face enhanced obligations for sensitive data processing.

training_data_transparency.detail: Not addressed directly; general notice obligations cover data use.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: DPDPB enforcement up to ₹250 crore (≈$30M) per violation; DPDPB adjudicates complaints; no private right of action.

background.origin: India's decade-long data protection journey began with a 2017 Supreme Court ruling (Puttaswamy) affirming privacy as a fundamental right. The Justice Srikrishna Committee (2018) produced the first draft; three failed bills (PDP 2019, PDP 2021, DPDP 2022) preceded the enacted DPDPA 2023.
key_drafters: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
Rajeev Chandrasekhar (Minister of State for Electronics, 2023 bill)
Cyberlaw experts Pavan Duggal and Nappinai N.S. (consultants)
key_opposition: Civil liberties groups opposed broad government data access exemptions
Press freedom organisations over media exemptions rollback
Opposition parties over data localisation provisions dropped from final bill
unique_features: Data protection board model rather than independent regulator
Significant government exemption for national security — broader than GDPR
Consent Manager framework unique to Indian approach
Digital Nagriks (digital citizens) framing reflects constitutional rights lens
background.legislative_notes: PDP Bill 2019 lapsed when Parliament dissolved. 2021 revision withdrawn after JPC report suggested 81 amendments. 2022 draft exposed for public comment. Final DPDPA introduced and passed in August 2023 in both Houses in under two days, drawing criticism for insufficient debate.

implementation_phases.description: DPDPA enacted
Data Protection Board notification issued
Draft DPDP Rules published for consultation
Expected commencement of key provisions upon rules finalisation

operative_dates: Act enacted Aug 2023; operative provisions subject to commencement notification by the Central Government. Rules (2025 draft) have separate consultation timeline.

full_name: Online Safety (Relief and Accountability) Act 2025
max_penalty: Stop-communication directions; account-restriction directions; platform sanctions
preemption_notes: National law; Singapore is a unitary state with no sub-national preemption dynamic. IMDA oversees compliance.
summary: Establishes statutory causes of action and administrative powers targeting online harms including AI-generated deepfakes and synthetic media. Covers 13 categories of harmful content. The Online Safety Commission can issue stop-communication and account-restriction directions against platforms hosting AI-generated harmful content.
legal_citation: Online Safety (Relief) Act 2025 (Singapore)
key_obligations: Platforms must implement technical measures to prevent AI-generated CSAM
Designated online services must conduct risk assessments for AI-generated harms
Provide users with tools to reduce exposure to AI-generated harmful content
IMDA enforcement with significant civil penalties for non-compliance

impact_assessment.detail: Online platforms must conduct content risk assessments and implement systems to prevent harmful AI-generated content; IMDA may require independent audits.

prohibited_categories.detail: Platform safety law; no AI application prohibitions.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: IMDA enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: Online services must implement systems to detect and remove AI-generated harmful content including NCII deepfakes; criminal offense for distributing non-consensual intimate AI images.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: IMDA enforcement; fines up to S$1M; criminal liability for severe violations; blocking orders for non-compliant platforms.

full_name: Federal Labor Law and Federal Copyright Law Amendments — AI Voice and Image Rights
summary: Requires explicit free and informed consent before AI systems use a person's voice or image in media. Mandates remuneration for consented use. Covers voice cloning, deepfakes, and generative models. Passed 335-129 in Chamber of Deputies. First Latin American law directly regulating AI voice/image rights.
notable: corpus boundary case — verify inclusion; first Latin American AI voice/image rights law. Passed same week as US TAKE IT DOWN Act.
legal_citation: Decreto por el que se adiciona el Artículo 132 Bis de la Ley Federal del Trabajo (2026)
key_obligations: Employers cannot use AI to replicate worker voice or image without explicit written consent
Workers have right to refuse AI likeness reproduction for commercial use
Labour law remedies apply for unauthorised AI use of worker identity

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Workers subject to AI-assisted performance evaluation, discipline, or termination decisions have the right to request human review and explanation.

private_right_of_action.detail: STPS and labor tribunal enforcement; existing labor dispute mechanisms apply.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed specifically.

anti_discrimination.detail: Requires AI in labor contexts to comply with non-discrimination principles; enforcement through existing labor law and Federal Labor Law.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: STPS and labor tribunal enforcement; fines and reinstatement orders for violations.

full_name: National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020
max_penalty: None — Framework statute establishing coordination; no enforcement penalties.
summary: The foundational US federal AI law, enacted as Division E of the FY2021 NDAA. Establishes the National AI Initiative to coordinate federal AI R&D, creates the National AI Initiative Office within OSTP, requires a National AI Research Resource, and mandates an AI technical standards program at NIST. Sets the institutional framework for subsequent federal AI governance.
notable: Provided the institutional scaffolding for subsequent Biden EO 14110 and the AI Safety Institute. First binding federal AI coordination statute.
legal_citation: Pub. L. 116-283, Div. E, §§ 5001–5901 (National AI Initiative Act)
key_obligations: Establishes National AI Initiative Office in OSTP to coordinate federal AI activities
NIST to develop voluntary AI standards and frameworks
NSF and DOE to expand AI research investments
National AI Research Resource to democratize access to AI compute and data
Annual report to Congress on federal AI R&D spending

impact_assessment.detail: R&D authorization act; no mandatory impact assessments for private sector.

prohibited_categories.detail: Research and coordination framework only; no prohibitions.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: No private enforcement.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Established the National AI Initiative as a coordinating body; focused on R&D investment, not product-level risk tiers.

enforcement_model.detail: Authorizing legislation with no penalties.

background.origin: Grew from the 2018 National AI Initiative coordination effort under OSTP and the bipartisan recognition that US AI policy was fragmented across agencies. Influenced by NIST AI standards work and the concern that the US lacked a coherent federal AI governance structure comparable to emerging EU and Chinese frameworks.
key_drafters: Rep. Eddie Bernice Johnson (D-TX, House version)
key_opposition: Libertarian-leaning members concerned about federal AI coordination as precursor to regulation
unique_features: Codifies a permanent National AI Initiative to coordinate federal AI R&D across agencies
Establishes the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) mandate
Creates interagency AI coordination committee within OSTP
Division E of the FY2021 NDAA — embedded in defence authorisation to ensure passage
Sets foundation for all subsequent US federal AI activity including Biden and Trump executive orders
background.legislative_notes: Introduced as standalone bill multiple sessions before being embedded in the FY2021 National Defence Authorisation Act (NDAA); signed January 1, 2021. Often considered the foundational US federal AI governance instrument despite its narrow scope.

full_name: Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits Act of 2024
max_penalty: Up to 10 years imprisonment (criminal); actual damages + attorney fees (civil)
preemption_notes: Federal civil remedy; does not preempt state NCII laws
summary: Creates a federal civil cause of action for victims of non-consensual intimate digital forgeries (AI-generated NCII). Plaintiffs may sue any person who knowingly produces or possesses NCII with intent to distribute when they know or recklessly disregard that the depicted person did not consent. Allows injunctive relief, actual damages, and attorney fees. Also creates criminal liability under 18 U.S.C.
notable: Predates TAKE IT DOWN Act; provides civil remedy whereas TAKE IT DOWN addresses platform takedown obligations. Together they form the US federal framework for AI-generated NCII.
legal_citation: S. 4569, 118th Cong. (2024); amends 18 U.S.C. § 2252E et seq.
key_obligations: Civil cause of action for victims of NCII deepfakes
Defendant liable if they knowingly produce or possess NCII with intent to distribute
Injunctive relief and actual damages available
Criminal penalties under amended federal statute

impact_assessment.detail: Targeted civil rights statute; no assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not prohibit AI uses per se; creates civil liability for harms.

human_review_rights.detail: No human review provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Victims may sue for actual damages, compensatory damages including pain and suffering, punitive damages up to $150,000, and attorney fees.

synthetic_media.detail: Provides federal civil cause of action for non-consensual intimate images including AI-generated deepfakes; covers distribution and receipt.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Civil damages remedy plus coordination with TAKE IT DOWN Act criminal framework; no standalone criminal penalties.

background.origin: The DEFIANCE Act (Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits) was triggered by the January 2024 viral spread of AI-generated non-consensual intimate images (NCII) of Taylor Swift on X (Twitter), reaching over 45 million views before removal. The incident created immediate congressional momentum for a federal civil remedy for AI-generated NCII. Sen. Dick Durbin and Rep. María Elvira Salazar introduced companion bills within weeks of the incident.
key_advocates: National Center for Missing and Exploited Children
key_opposition: No significant organised opposition — rare bipartisan consensus driven by public outrage
unique_features: Signed in the fastest legislative timeline of any major AI bill — from introduction to enactment in approximately 90 days
First federal civil right of action specifically for AI-generated intimate imagery
Creates a 10-year statute of limitations (much longer than typical tort claims)
Provides for liquidated damages of $150,000 per violation plus attorneys' fees — significant deterrent without requiring proof of actual harm
Inspired by the Taylor Swift viral deepfake incident of January 2024, making it the first celebrity-incident-triggered AI legislation at federal level
background.legislative_notes: Introduced February 2024; passed both chambers with overwhelming bipartisan support by June 2024; signed into law July 2024 by President Biden. The Taylor Swift incident catalysed legislative action that had stalled for years under the Stop NCII Act and similar proposals. Signed alongside a companion measure providing funding for Cyber Civil Rights Initiative hotline.

full_name: Use of Digital Replicas of Deceased Performers Act
max_penalty: Actual damages or $75,000 per violation; punitive damages available
summary: Extends California right of publicity protections to deceased performers by requiring prior consent from the estate before creating or using an AI-generated digital replica of a deceased performer in an audiovisual work, sound recording, or live performance. Applies to performances and recordings made during the performer's life.
notable: Part of a broader 2024 California AI legislative package targeting entertainment industry AI use. Signed by Governor Newsom.
legal_citation: Cal. Lab. Code §§ 3344.1 (as amended); AB 1836, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: Prior consent from estate required to create AI digital replica of deceased performer
Applies to audiovisual works, sound recordings, and live performances
Civil cause of action with actual damages or $75,000 per violation
Estate holds rights for 70 years post-death

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not prohibit AI categories; creates civil liability for unauthorized digital replicas.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Performers and estates may sue for actual damages, disgorgement, punitive damages, and attorney fees for unauthorized AI replicas.

synthetic_media.detail: Requires consent to create AI replicas of deceased performers; grants estates the right to license and control digital replicas for 70 years.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed separately; focuses on likeness/voice rather than biometric data.

content_labeling.detail: No labeling requirement; consent and liability focused.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Civil damages plus potential misappropriation claims; no standalone criminal penalties but coordinated with existing right of publicity law.

full_name: Contracts Involving AI Replicas of Performers Act
max_penalty: Contract unenforceable; civil damages
summary: Voids provisions in entertainment contracts that grant employers the right to use an AI replica of a performer to replace work the performer would otherwise perform, unless the performer receives specific, individualized notice and representation by a qualified representative. Applies to contracts for audiovisual and sound recording work.
notable: Labor protections for performers against AI replacement in contracts. Companion bill to AB 1836 on the employment side.
legal_citation: Cal. Lab. Code § 3344.1(c) (as amended); AB 2602, 2023–24 Leg. Sess.
key_obligations: AI replica contract provisions unenforceable unless performer receives individual notice
Performer must be represented by qualified representative before signing AI replica rights away
Applies to contracts for audiovisual and recorded performance work

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Performers may void contracts that purport to give AI rights to their voice/likeness without specific disclosure; remedies include damages.

synthetic_media.detail: Voids contract provisions that give AI rights to a performer's likeness or voice without explicit individual negotiation and disclosure; contracts must specify each AI use.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed separately.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Civil contract voiding mechanism; no criminal penalties.

full_name: Minnesota Artificial Intelligence and Elections Disclosure Act
max_penalty: Civil action; up to $1,000 per violation or actual damages
summary: Prohibits the creation or distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated audio or visual media depicting a political candidate within 90 days of an election without a disclosure label. Requires prominent disclosure that content is AI-generated. Provides private right of action for candidates.
notable: One of a wave of 2024 state laws targeting AI-generated deepfake election content. Minnesota was an early mover.
legal_citation: Minn. Stat. § 211B.17 (as amended); HF 4114, 2024 Minn. Leg.
key_obligations: Disclosure label required on AI-generated political media within 90 days of election
Prohibition on materially deceptive AI-generated candidate depictions without disclosure
Private right of action for affected candidates
Platform liability for knowing distribution of non-disclosed AI election content

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits dissemination of AI-generated deepfakes depicting political candidates within 90 days of an election without prominent disclosure.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Depicted candidates may seek injunctive relief and damages for election deepfakes published without disclosure.

synthetic_media.detail: AI-generated election-related content must include prominent disclosure; criminal prohibition on undisclosed deepfakes of candidates.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: Mandatory disclosure label on AI-generated political content; applies to candidate depictions in election advertising.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal misdemeanor for undisclosed election deepfakes plus civil remedy for depicted candidates; AG enforcement.

full_name: Florida Deceptive AI Content in Political Advertising Act
max_penalty: $1,000 per day for political committee non-disclosure violations
summary: Requires political advertisements containing AI-generated content to include a clear and conspicuous disclosure stating the content was "created in whole or in part with the use of generative artificial intelligence." Applies to television, radio, digital, and print political advertising in Florida.
notable: Governor DeSantis signed this while vetoing a broader AI bill. Florida takes a narrow, disclosure-only approach to AI in elections.
key_obligations: Political ads containing AI-generated content must include prominent disclosure label
Disclosure must state content was created using generative AI
Applies to all political advertising formats: TV, radio, digital, print
Division of Elections enforcement

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits AI-generated political advertisements without disclosure; bans AI-generated deepfakes of political candidates without prominent labeling.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Candidates depicted in undisclosed deepfakes may seek injunctive relief.

synthetic_media.detail: All political advertisements using AI-generated content must include a disclosure; applies to AI-created, altered, or doctored images, video, or audio of candidates.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: Political AI content must display "Created in whole or in part with the use of generative artificial intelligence" label.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal violation for non-compliant AI political ads; Florida Election Commission enforcement plus candidate civil remedy.

full_name: Georgia Artificial Intelligence in Creative Content Act
max_penalty: Actual damages; injunctive relief
summary: Extends Georgia's right of publicity statute to prohibit the creation of AI-generated synthetic depictions of individuals' likeness or voice without consent for commercial purposes. Provides civil remedies including actual damages and injunctive relief. Focuses on performers and artists in the entertainment industry.
notable: Part of the entertainment industry-driven wave of 2024 AI likeness protection laws. Georgia is home to a major film and music industry.
legal_citation: Ga. Code Ann. §§ 51-5-1 to 51-5-10 (as amended); SB 396, 2024 Ga. Gen. Assem.
key_obligations: Consent required before creating AI depiction of individual likeness or voice for commercial use
Civil cause of action: actual damages and injunctive relief
Applies to synthetic audio and visual depictions in commercial contexts

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Not addressed.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Individuals may sue for actual damages, disgorgement, injunction, and attorney fees for unauthorized AI replicas of their likeness or voice.

synthetic_media.detail: Extends Georgia right of publicity to AI-generated replicas; requires consent for AI replication of voice, image, or likeness for commercial use.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Civil remedy (actual damages, disgorgement, injunction); no standalone criminal penalty.

full_name: Indiana Deceptive AI Political Content Prohibition Act
max_penalty: $1,000 per violation
summary: Prohibits the distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated audio or visual media depicting a candidate within 90 days before an election without clear disclosure. Requires a disclosure label stating the content is AI-generated. Indiana Election Commission may impose civil penalties.
legal_citation: Ind. Code § 3-14-3-3.5; SB 10, 2024 Ind. Gen. Assem.
key_obligations: Prohibition on distributing materially deceptive AI political content within 90 days of election
Disclosure label required on AI-generated political content
Indiana Election Commission civil penalty enforcement

impact_assessment.detail: Not addressed.

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits knowingly disseminating AI-generated deepfake audio or video depicting Indiana candidates within 90 days of an election without disclosure.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: State enforcement only.

synthetic_media.detail: AI-generated election content must be labeled; undisclosed deepfakes depicting candidates are prohibited.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

content_labeling.detail: AI-generated political content must include clear disclosure label.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

max_penalty: Civil rights damages under Illinois Human Rights Act

key_obligations: Notify candidates when AI analytics tools are used in screening
Annual report to state on race/ethnicity demographics of candidates reviewed by AI
Comply with Illinois Human Rights Act anti-discrimination requirements

enforcement_model.detail: IDHR enforcement under Illinois Human Rights Act framework; civil penalties.

full_name: North Carolina Protecting Elections from Deceptive AI Act
enforcement_body: North Carolina State Board of Elections
max_penalty: Class 2 misdemeanor; campaign finance violation penalties

Disclosure must state content is AI-generated
Class 2 misdemeanor for knowing violations

enforcement_model.detail: State elections board enforcement; civil penalties.

max_penalty: Category E felony (criminal) for deceptive election deepfakes
summary: Prohibits the knowing distribution of materially deceptive AI-generated media depicting a candidate within 60 days of an election without disclosure. notable: Category E felony for knowing violation makes Nevada one of the strictest states on AI election deepfakes.
legal_citation: NRS § 294A.400 et seq.; AB 384, 82nd Nev. Leg. (2024)
key_obligations: Prohibition on distributing deceptive AI election media within 60 days of election
Disclosure label required on AI-generated political content
Category E felony for knowing violations

full_name: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 on Liability for Defective Products
max_penalty: Full compensation for damages (no cap)
preemption_notes: Replaces 1985 Product Liability Directive (85/374/EEC); harmonizes EU member state product liability
summary: Modernises EU product liability rules to cover AI systems and software. Clarifies that AI systems are "products" under EU law; manufacturers and importers are strictly liable for damage caused by defective AI products. Introduces disclosure obligations for defendants to share technical documentation, alleviating the burden of proof problem for victims of AI harms.
notable: Companion to EU AI Act — the AI Act sets ex ante regulatory requirements; the revised PLD creates the ex post civil liability pathway for AI harm. Together they form the EU AI liability framework.
key_obligations: AI systems are "products" — manufacturers strictly liable for defective AI causing damage
Defendants must disclose technical documentation when requested by plaintiff courts
Presumption of causation where defect is plausible and damage consistent with type
Member states must implement by December 9, 2026

impact_assessment.detail: Liability statute; no obligation to conduct impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: Liability statute; does not prohibit AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: Core mechanism: treats AI systems as "products" — defective AI causing physical or significant non-material harm triggers strict liability without proving fault.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Not addressed.

enforcement_model.detail: Civil courts enforce claims; no administrative penalties — damages flowing from defective AI products adjudicated through national court systems.

full_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 on Cybersecurity Requirements for Products with Digital Elements
max_penalty: €15,000,000 or 2.5% of global annual turnover (whichever higher)
preemption_notes: Harmonises EU cybersecurity requirements for digital products
summary: Establishes mandatory cybersecurity requirements for all products with digital elements placed on the EU market, including AI systems. Manufacturers must conduct security risk assessments, implement security-by-design, provide security updates throughout product lifecycle, and report actively exploited vulnerabilities within 24 hours. AI systems that are "products with digital elements" must comply alongside AI Act requirements.
notable: The CRA applies to AI systems as products with digital elements, creating overlapping obligations with the EU AI Act. Critical AI products require third-party security assessment.
key_obligations: Security risk assessment required before market placement
Implement security-by-design and security-by-default
Provide security updates throughout product lifecycle (minimum 5 years)
Report exploited vulnerabilities to ENISA within 24 hours
Critical products require third-party conformity assessment

impact_assessment.detail: Manufacturers of products with digital elements (including AI) must conduct cybersecurity risk assessments before placing on market; critical products require third-party conformity assessment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Cybersecurity law; does not prohibit AI applications by category.

human_review_rights.detail: Not addressed.

private_right_of_action.detail: National market surveillance authorities enforce; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Not addressed.

risk_classification.detail: Risk classification by cybersecurity criticality, not AI application type.

enforcement_model.detail: Up to €15M or 2.5% global annual turnover for non-compliance; national market surveillance authorities enforce.

full_name: Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (Brazilian AI Framework Law)
max_penalty: R$50,000,000 per violation (~$9M USD) or 2% of revenue
preemption_notes: Federal law; supersedes conflicting state-level rules. ANPD, CADE, and sector regulators share enforcement. State-level AI rules must align with federal framework.
summary: Brazil's comprehensive AI framework law, passed after three years of parliamentary debate. Establishes a risk-based regulatory regime modeled partly on the EU AI Act. Creates prohibited AI categories, mandates impact assessments for high-risk AI, requires AI interaction disclosure, and grants individuals rights to contest AI decisions. ANPD is the primary enforcement authority alongside sector regulators.
notable: First comprehensive AI framework law in Latin America. Effective January 1, 2026. ANPD must issue implementing regulations within 180 days of enactment.
legal_citation: Lei n° 2338/2023 (enacted 2025) — Marco Legal da IA (Brazil)
key_obligations: Disclosure required when interacting with AI system
High-risk AI systems require prior algorithmic impact assessment
Prohibited AI categories include social scoring and manipulative AI
Human review right for AI decisions with significant effects
Private right of action for individuals harmed by prohibited AI
AI providers must register high-risk systems with ANPD

impact_assessment.detail: Providers and operators of high-risk AI must conduct impact assessments addressing fundamental rights, data protection, and discriminatory effects; assessments must be filed with ANPD.

prohibited_categories.detail: High-risk framework; specific prohibited categories addressed in implementing regulations.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have the right to request human review and explanation of any consequential AI decision; operators must respond within reasonable timeframe.

private_right_of_action.detail: ANPD enforcement; no direct private right of action in the AI Act.

synthetic_media.detail: Not addressed in the AI Act; covered by separate digital rights framework.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is sensitive data under LGPD; Brazil AI Act incorporates LGPD consent requirements; heightened standards for biometric AI applications.

anti_discrimination.detail: AI systems must not produce discriminatory effects on protected groups; operators must monitor and mitigate disparate impacts; impact-based standard.

risk_classification.detail: High-risk AI system classification in 8 sectors (credit, employment, education, healthcare, public services, housing, immigration, justice); binary with binding obligations.

enforcement_model.detail: ANPD enforcement up to R$50M or 2% of Brazilian revenues; coordinated with LGPD liability framework.

background.origin: Emerged from Brazil's early AI policy debate starting in 2019, catalysed by LGPD (2018) and international pressure from EU AI Act development. Senate Bill 2338 was the culmination of five competing bills merged by a special parliamentary committee.
key_drafters: ITS Rio (Institute of Technology and Society, technical consultant)
key_opposition: Big Tech companies (Google, Meta, Microsoft) opposing liability provisions
Startups concerned about compliance costs
Fintech sector lobbying for sector-specific carve-outs
unique_features: First Global South country to pass comprehensive AI law
Explicit "AI developer" liability for foreseeable harm — broader than EU AI Act
Prohibits automated denial of credit, employment, or insurance without human review
Covers AI systems used outside Brazil if they affect Brazilian users
background.legislative_notes: Multiple bills filed 2019–2022; Senate created special committee in 2023; Bill 2338 passed Senate May 2024; House amended and returned; final text enacted with presidential signature in January 2025. President Lula used AI Act signing to signal Brazil's tech sovereignty ambitions.

implementation_phases.description: Brazil AI Act signed into law
General obligations take effect (6-month grace period)
High-risk AI system obligations and conformity assessments required
Full enforcement regime operational; ANPD regulatory guidance finalised

operative_dates: Published Jul 2025. General provisions: 180 days post-publication (Jan 2026). High-risk AI obligations: 24 months post-publication (Jul 2027).

full_name: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (India)
max_penalty: ₹250 crore (~$30M USD) per data protection board order
summary: Implementing rules under India's 2023 DPDPA establishing specific compliance requirements for significant data fiduciaries (large-scale data processors). Rules specify consent notice formats, data protection officer qualifications, data impact assessment requirements, and Data Protection Board procedure. AI systems used by significant data fiduciaries must comply with assessment requirements.
notable: Rules complete the DPDPA framework. AI developers operating at scale in India qualify as significant data fiduciaries and face enhanced obligations.
legal_citation: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, MeitY Notification S.O. 2025
key_obligations: Significant data fiduciaries must appoint data protection officer
Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing
Specified consent notice format and language requirements
Audit and algorithmic assessment by independent data auditor annually
Implement privacy by design mechanisms in AI systems

prohibited_categories.detail: Implementing rules; no new prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Rules specify grievance mechanism timelines and procedures; data principals may challenge automated decisions within 30 days.

legal_citation: Legge 23 settembre 2025, n. 132, Gazzetta Ufficiale n. 224 del 25-9-2025

max_penalty: £17.5M or 4% of global turnover
preemption_notes: UK diverges from EU GDPR on automated decisions; replaces near-prohibition with permission+safeguards framework
