impact_assessment.detail: No impact assessment requirements; amends existing Utah AI Policy Act disclosure obligations.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibitions; extends disclosure and transparency requirements to licensed professions.

human_review_rights.detail: Consumers may inquire whether a professional is using AI; no formal human review right.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement through Utah Division of Consumer Protection and AG; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Does not address biometric data.

content_labeling.detail: Licensed professionals (lawyers, healthcare providers, financial advisers) must disclose AI use to consumers upon request.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; disclosure obligations apply uniformly across regulated professions.

full_name: Security Management Measures for the Application of Facial Recognition Technology
max_penalty: Administrative penalty: up to CNY 1,000,000 (~$140,000) for serious violations; CNY 50,000 for minor
preemption_notes: National standard and regulation issued by CAC; applies across all Chinese jurisdictions. Sub-national AI facial recognition rules (e.g., Shanghai) must align.
summary: Regulates the application of facial recognition technology in China. Requires explicit consent for facial recognition, limits its use to genuinely necessary scenarios, mandates security assessments for systems processing large volumes of facial data, and prohibits unlawful use for personal identification without consent. Public-space deployments require state approval and must display notices.
notable: First dedicated facial recognition regulation in China; prohibits use in hotel rooms, public baths, and other sensitive venues. Security assessment required for systems processing 100,000+ facial records.
legal_citation: Security Management Measures for Facial Recognition Technology, CAC Order No. 22 (2024)
key_obligations: Obtain explicit written consent before collecting facial data
Display visible notices when facial recognition is deployed in public
Conduct security assessments for systems processing 100,000+ people
Prohibit facial recognition in hotel rooms, changing rooms, restrooms
Delete facial data when original purpose is fulfilled

impact_assessment.detail: Security assessment required before deploying systems processing 100,000+ facial records

prohibited_categories.detail: Prohibits facial recognition in hotel rooms, changing rooms, toilets, and other sensitive venues without state approval

human_review_rights.detail: Consequential decisions based on facial recognition (access control, benefits, security) require human review before final determination.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement is administrative through CAC; no private right of action, though civil tort claims under PIPL are available separately.

synthetic_media.detail: Regulation addresses facial recognition authentication; does not cover synthetic face generation.

biometric_data.detail: Explicit written consent required before any collection of facial biometric data; consent cannot be bundled with service terms

training_data_transparency.detail: Training data for facial recognition systems must meet quality, accuracy, and consent compliance standards; data provenance records required.

content_labeling.detail: Does not address content labeling; focused on authentication use cases.

anti_discrimination.detail: No explicit anti-discrimination standard; accuracy requirements imply fairness but no formal disparate impact analysis required.

risk_classification.detail: Applications classified by sensitivity: financial, law enforcement, and public security uses subject to highest requirements; consumer uses to lower tier.

enforcement_model.detail: CAC and MPS administrative enforcement; fines up to RMB 1M and business suspension

short_name: China Scientific and Technological Ethics Review
full_name: Measures for Scientific and Technological Ethics Review
max_penalty: None — Ethics framework; penalties imposed through institutional review, not monetary fines.
summary: Requires scientific and technological research institutions to conduct ethics reviews for AI research activities. Establishes ethics review committees at research institutions, mandates pre-project ethics review for high-risk research affecting human rights or societal values, and creates a tiered review process with escalation for sensitive research involving AI, life sciences, and data.
notable: Applies to universities and research institutions; AI research involving personal data or automated decision-making must undergo formal ethics committee review before commencing.
legal_citation: Measures for Scientific and Technological Ethics Review, MOST Order (2023)
key_obligations: Establish ethics review committees at research institutions
Conduct mandatory ethics review for AI research affecting human rights or safety
Escalate high-risk research to national-level review
Document and report ethics review outcomes

impact_assessment.detail: Mandatory pre-project ethics review at institutional committee level for AI research involving personal data, life sciences, or societal risk

prohibited_categories.detail: Research activities that threaten national security, undermine social stability, or violate core socialist values are prohibited.

human_review_rights.detail: Institutional ethics review framework; no individual human review rights for affected persons.

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative enforcement through institutional review committees and MOST; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Ethics framework for scientific research; does not specifically address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: General ethics framework; biometric data addressed under PIPL separately.

training_data_transparency.detail: Scientific research ethics framework; training data disclosure addressed separately under GenAI and Deep Synthesis regulations.

anti_discrimination.detail: Ethics framework does not create an anti-discrimination standard; focuses on research process integrity.

risk_classification.detail: Tiered ethics review: institutional committee for standard research, escalation to national-level review for high-risk research affecting national security or public safety

enforcement_model.detail: Institutional ethics committee review with referral to MOST; no published penalty schedule or enforcement model comparable to other regulations.

full_name: Shenzhen Special Economic Zone Artificial Intelligence Industry Promotion Regulation
max_penalty: None — Promotion ordinance; penalties deferredto national regulations.
preemption_notes: Sub-national SEZ regulation; national regulations take precedence
summary: China's first sub-national comprehensive AI regulation, enacted by Shenzhen's Special Economic Zone legislature. Covers the full lifecycle of AI development, promotion, governance, and accountability. Requires AI providers in specified domains to conduct algorithmic impact assessments, disclose AI use to affected parties, and allow human review of automated decisions. Includes innovation incentives alongside governance obligations.
notable: First city-level AI regulation in China; served as a policy test-bed for national AI rules and has stronger algorithmic accountability provisions than most national regulations at the time of enactment.
legal_citation: Shenzhen SEZ AI Industry Promotion Regulation (2022)
key_obligations: Conduct algorithmic impact assessments for high-risk AI systems
Disclose AI use to affected individuals in specified sectors
Provide human review option for automated decisions in key domains
Register AI systems with Shenzhen municipal authorities
Comply with data security and personal information protection requirements

impact_assessment.detail: Algorithmic impact assessments required before deployment in specified high-risk domains including employment, education, and healthcare

prohibited_categories.detail: Promotion ordinance designed to attract AI industry; no prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals may request human review of automated decisions in key domains including government services and employment

private_right_of_action.detail: Industry promotion ordinance; enforcement is through regulatory compliance, not individual rights.

synthetic_media.detail: No synthetic media provisions; promotion-focused legislation.

biometric_data.detail: No specific biometric provisions; national PIPL and CAC regulations govern.

training_data_transparency.detail: AI providers must file technical documentation about training data sources and quality with Shenzhen authorities

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling requirements; defers to national GenAI and Deep Synthesis regulations.

anti_discrimination.detail: Impact assessments must include bias and fairness analysis; operators must take reasonable steps to prevent discriminatory outcomes

risk_classification.detail: Distinguishes high-risk AI systems (government services, healthcare, employment, education) subject to heightened obligations from lower-risk systems

enforcement_model.detail: Shenzhen municipal enforcement with administrative penalties and business suspension; safe harbor for operators who conduct assessments

full_name: Ley que Promueve el Uso Responsable de la Inteligencia Artificial en el Peru (Law No. 31814)
enforcement_body: PCM (Presidency of the Council of Ministers)
Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation
max_penalty: None — Framework governance law; penalty amounts set in implementing regulation SD 115-2025.
summary: Peru's AI governance law promotes responsible development and use of AI while protecting fundamental rights. Establishes principles of non-discrimination, privacy, human oversight, transparency, sustainability, accountability, and intellectual property respect. Public institutions must register AI systems and conduct impact assessments. AI systems used in high-stakes decisions affecting citizens must provide human review options.
notable: One of Latin America's first dedicated AI governance laws, predating Brazil's AI Act by two years. Establishes a national AI framework centered on human rights and public sector accountability.
legal_citation: Ley N 31814, Diario Oficial El Peruano (2023)
key_obligations: Register AI systems used in public sector decisions with PCM
Conduct impact assessments for AI systems affecting citizens rights
Provide human review for automated decisions in high-stakes contexts
Disclose AI use to affected individuals
Ensure non-discrimination in AI system design and deployment

impact_assessment.detail: Public institutions must conduct AI impact assessments before deploying AI systems that affect citizens' rights or access to public services

prohibited_categories.detail: Framework governance law; establishes regulatory institutions and principles without defining prohibited AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Citizens have the right to human review of automated decisions that significantly affect their access to public services

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative enforcement through INDECOPI and sector regulators; no private right of action established.

synthetic_media.detail: General AI governance framework; does not specifically address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No specific biometric provisions; addressed under Peru's data protection law separately.

training_data_transparency.detail: Framework law; training data requirements to be developed through implementing regulations.

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling provisions; to be addressed in implementing regulations.

anti_discrimination.detail: Non-discrimination principle established but enforcement defers to existing constitutional and civil rights frameworks

risk_classification.detail: Law establishes binary classification: high-risk AI (requiring conformity assessment) vs. other AI; similar to early EU approach.

enforcement_model.detail: INDECOPI and sectoral regulators enforce; administrative penalties with graduated fines for non-compliance.

full_name: Directive on Automated Decision-Making
max_penalty: None — Internal government directive; enforced by Treasury Board audit, no monetary penalty.
preemption_notes: Applies only to federal government institutions; no private sector obligations
summary: Canada's Treasury Board directive requires federal government institutions to assess and document the impact of automated decision systems before deploying them. Uses a tiered impact level system (I-IV) where higher-impact systems require peer review, algorithmic impact assessments, human review options, and explanations to affected parties. Level IV systems (highest impact) require ministerial approval. One of the first binding automated-decision governance rules for a national government.
notable: Pioneering federal AI accountability framework predating the EU AI Act and most national AI laws; influenced similar directives in the UK and Australia for public sector AI.
legal_citation: Directive on Automated Decision-Making, Treasury Board of Canada (2019, updated 2023)
key_obligations: Complete Algorithmic Impact Assessment before deploying automated decision systems
Apply tiered obligations based on impact level (I-IV)
Provide human review option for Level II+ systems
Explain automated decisions to affected parties on request
Obtain ministerial approval for Level IV (highest impact) systems
Log all automated decisions for audit purposes

impact_assessment.detail: Algorithmic Impact Assessment mandatory before any automated decision system deployment; must be publicly released for Level II+ systems

prohibited_categories.detail: Government internal directive; does not define prohibited categories, focuses on due process for existing automated decision uses.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have the right to human review and explanation for any decision made by a Level II or higher automated system; review must be meaningful and result in a new decision

private_right_of_action.detail: Internal administrative directive; enforceable through Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat audit, not individual litigation.

synthetic_media.detail: Applies to government automated decision-making; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No specific biometric data provisions; covered under Privacy Act separately.

training_data_transparency.detail: Does not require training data disclosure; focuses on algorithmic impact assessment and human review.

anti_discrimination.detail: AIA template includes mandatory bias assessment across protected characteristics; operators must implement mitigations for disparate impact identified in the assessment

risk_classification.detail: Four-tier impact levels (I-IV) with binding obligations escalating by tier; Level IV requires ministerial approval and peer review; one of the first government ADM risk frameworks

enforcement_model.detail: Internal Treasury Board compliance mechanism; no penalties but directive is binding on all federal departments; compliance audited by TBS

full_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on Harmonised Rules on Fair Access to and Use of Data (Data Act)
max_penalty: Up to 1% of global annual turnover
preemption_notes: Directly applicable EU regulation; preempts conflicting member state rules on data sharing and access
summary: The EU Data Act establishes harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data generated by connected products (IoT) and related services across the EU. Key AI implications include: users gain access to data generated by AI-enabled products; rules restrict cloud-switching lock-in affecting AI infrastructure; data sharing with public bodies in emergencies is mandated; and AI model vendors cannot exploit IoT device data without user consent.
notable: Governs data from AI-connected devices and smart products; acts as the data portability companion to the EU AI Act. Became fully effective September 2025.
legal_citation: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854, OJ L, 22 December 2023
key_obligations: Connected product manufacturers must give users access to device-generated data
Data holders must share data with users and authorised third parties on request
Cloud service providers must enable data portability and switching within 30 days
Prohibit AI model vendors from using non-personal IoT data without explicit agreement
Public bodies may request emergency data access in declared crises

impact_assessment.detail: Data Act addresses data access and portability; does not require AI impact assessments (addressed under EU AI Act separately).

prohibited_categories.detail: Enables and governs data sharing; does not prohibit categories of AI use.

human_review_rights.detail: Data portability and access rights are distinct from automated decision-making human review rights under GDPR Art. 22.

private_right_of_action.detail: Civil liability for damages arising from defective data products and services; complements EU Product Liability Directive pathway.

synthetic_media.detail: Data portability law; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data is excluded from mandatory sharing obligations as sensitive data; addressed under GDPR separately.

training_data_transparency.detail: Data holders must share IoT-generated data with users and authorised third parties; AI vendors cannot exploit device data without explicit agreement, creating a de-facto training data consent mechanism for connected-device data

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination provisions; data access framework is neutral on outcomes.

risk_classification.detail: No AI risk classification; risk framework is addressed under EU AI Act.

enforcement_model.detail: National market surveillance authorities enforce; penalties up to 1% of global turnover; cloud providers face injunctions for non-compliance with switching obligations

full_name: Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025 (Bangladesh)
max_penalty: Administrative penalty: up to BDT 5,000,000 (~$45,000); criminal penalties for deliberate violations
summary: Bangladesh's first personal data protection law. AI-relevant provisions include: data protection impact assessments required for high-risk processing (including profiling and automated decision-making), individuals have the right to object to purely automated decisions affecting their legal rights, and biometric and health data are classified as sensitive categories requiring explicit consent.
notable: First data protection law in Bangladesh; the automated decision-making provisions follow the GDPR Article 22 model.
legal_citation: Personal Data Protection Ordinance 2025, Bangladesh Gazette
key_obligations: Obtain explicit consent for processing sensitive personal data including biometrics
Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk AI processing
Provide individuals the right to object to purely automated decisions
Appoint a Data Protection Officer for high-risk processing
Report data breaches to the Data Protection Authority within prescribed timeframes

impact_assessment.detail: Data Protection Impact Assessment required for high-risk processing including AI profiling and automated decision-making affecting legal rights

prohibited_categories.detail: Data protection ordinance; no AI-specific prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Right to object to purely automated decisions affecting legal interests, modeled on GDPR Article 22; controller must carry out human review on request

private_right_of_action.detail: Data subjects may seek compensation for damages from controllers who violate their rights; injunctive relief available through courts.

synthetic_media.detail: Data protection framework; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric and health data classified as sensitive personal data requiring explicit, separate consent; cannot be bundled with general service terms

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; focuses on lawful basis for personal data processing.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory automated processing not explicitly addressed; defers to Bangladesh's existing equality and discrimination frameworks.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework; data protection principles apply uniformly.

enforcement_model.detail: Penalties established in ordinance but quantum not yet determined by regulation; enforcement by Bangladesh Data Protection Authority once established

full_name: Ley Estatutaria 1581 de 2012 — Proteccion de Datos Personales
max_penalty: Up to 2,000 SMLMV (approx. USD 700K)
summary: Colombia's foundational data protection law establishing rights and obligations for personal data processing. Applied to AI systems by the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC) through regulatory guidance on algorithmic systems and automated profiling. Requires consent for personal data processing, provides access and rectification rights, and protects sensitive categories including biometric data. The SIC has issued specific guidance on AI systems under this law.
notable: Applied to AI by SIC administrative guidance; Colombia's regulator has been among Latin America's most proactive in applying data protection rules to AI and profiling systems.
legal_citation: Ley 1581 de 2012, Diario Oficial No. 48.587
key_obligations: Obtain prior, express, and informed consent for personal data processing
Provide data subjects with access, correction, and deletion rights
Register databases containing personal data with the SIC
Classify sensitive data (health, biometric, political) and apply heightened protections
Notify data subjects and SIC of data breaches

impact_assessment.detail: 2012 law predates AI impact assessment concepts; no data protection impact assessment requirement.

prohibited_categories.detail: General data protection law; focuses on lawful basis for processing rather than prohibited AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Data subjects have right to know about automated processing (habeas data); explanation available but no explicit right to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Constitutional habeas data action available plus civil damages under Colombian tort law for data protection violations.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric and health data classified as sensitive personal data under SIC guidance; requires explicit consent and cannot be used for purposes beyond original collection

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; 2012 law predates ML training data concerns.

anti_discrimination.detail: Non-discrimination applies through general data processing principles; SIC guidance on AI profiling references existing anti-discrimination law but does not add new standards

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; data protection obligations apply based on data sensitivity, not AI risk level.

enforcement_model.detail: SIC can impose fines up to 2,000 SMLMV (~USD 700K) for serious violations; SIC has used this authority in AI-related profiling cases

short_name: Mauritius Financial Services AI Advisory Rules
full_name: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021
max_penalty: FSC enforcement: penalties per Financial Services Act; advisory rules — compliance notices
summary: Mauritius rules governing robo-advisory and AI-enabled financial advisory services. Requires licensed financial advisors deploying AI-powered advisory systems to disclose the automated nature of advice, ensure the system is fit for purpose, maintain human escalation options for clients, and conduct ongoing performance monitoring. One of the first sector-specific AI financial services regulations in Africa.
notable: First AI-specific financial services regulation in Africa; establishes a licensing and disclosure framework for robo-advisory services in Mauritius.
legal_citation: Financial Services (Robotic and AI Enabled Advisory Services) Rules 2021, FSC Mauritius
key_obligations: Disclose automated nature of advice to clients before onboarding
Maintain a human escalation pathway for complex advisory needs
Conduct regular assessments of AI advisory system performance
Ensure AI system aligns with client risk profiles
Obtain FSC approval before deploying robo-advisory services

impact_assessment.detail: Annual fitness-for-purpose assessments of AI advisory systems required; FSC must be notified of material changes to the AI model

prohibited_categories.detail: Advisory rules for financial services sector; no prohibited AI categories defined.

human_review_rights.detail: Human advisor escalation pathway mandatory for all robo-advisory deployments; clients must be able to access human advisor at any point in the advisory process

private_right_of_action.detail: FSC regulatory rules; enforcement is by the Financial Services Commission, not private litigation.

synthetic_media.detail: Financial services AI guidelines; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Advisory rules do not specifically address biometric data use in financial services.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data transparency requirements; advisory guidance focuses on governance and risk management.

anti_discrimination.detail: No explicit anti-discrimination standard; fairness principles implied in general guidance.

risk_classification.detail: Advisory framework; no formal binding risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: FSC administrative enforcement; license revocation is the primary sanction for robo-advisory compliance failures

full_name: DIFC Data Protection Regulation 10: Processing Personal Data Through Autonomous and Semi-Autonomous Systems
max_penalty: USD 100,000 per violation
preemption_notes: Applies within DIFC free zone only
summary: The Dubai International Financial Centre's dedicated regulation for AI and automated decision-making. Controllers using autonomous or semi-autonomous systems must conduct data protection impact assessments, notify individuals when significant decisions are made automatically, provide human review rights, and register high-risk autonomous systems with the DIFC Commissioner. One of the earliest standalone AI/automated-systems regulations in the Middle East.
notable: DIFC is Dubai's primary financial free zone; this regulation influenced UAE federal AI policy and similar rules in ADGM (Abu Dhabi Global Market).
legal_citation: DIFC Commissioner's Office, Regulation No. 10 of 2020
key_obligations: Conduct data protection impact assessment before deploying autonomous systems
Notify individuals when significant decisions are made autonomously
Provide human review option for autonomous decisions affecting rights or interests
Register high-risk autonomous systems with DIFC Commissioner
Maintain audit trails for all autonomous decisions

impact_assessment.detail: Data Protection Impact Assessment required before deploying any autonomous or semi-autonomous system that processes personal data

prohibited_categories.detail: Regulation focuses on liability and accountability for autonomous systems; does not define prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have the right to request human review of any significant decision made by an autonomous system; the review must result in a new, independent determination

private_right_of_action.detail: DIFC Courts provide civil liability pathway for harm caused by autonomous systems; actual damages available.

synthetic_media.detail: Autonomous systems regulation; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed separately under DIFC Data Protection Law 2020.

training_data_transparency.detail: Focuses on operator liability; no training data transparency requirements.

anti_discrimination.detail: No explicit anti-discrimination standard; DIFC Employment Law covers discrimination separately.

risk_classification.detail: High-risk autonomous systems must be registered with the DIFC Commissioner and undergo enhanced DPIA; lower-risk systems require standard DPIA only

enforcement_model.detail: DIFC Commissioner can impose fines up to USD 100,000 per violation; injunctions available

full_name: Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM — Implementing Regulations for Law 31814 on Responsible Use of AI
enforcement_body: Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation
max_penalty: Same penalty framework as Law 31814 — up to 150 UIT (~$210,000)
summary: Peru's first comprehensive AI implementing regulation under Law 31814. Establishes a risk classification framework (minimal, limited, high, unacceptable), defines prohibited AI practices, mandates transparency and human oversight for high-risk systems, extends obligations to the private sector, and creates a national AI registry. Covers both public institutions and private sector actors deploying AI systems that affect individuals' rights.
notable: Extends Peru's AI governance framework from public sector to private sector; defines unacceptable-risk AI systems modeled partly on the EU AI Act's prohibited practices list.
legal_citation: Decreto Supremo N 115-2025-PCM, El Peruano (Sept 2025)
key_obligations: Classify AI systems according to four-tier risk framework
Register high-risk AI systems in national AI registry
Conduct impact assessments for high-risk AI before deployment
Prohibit AI systems categorised as unacceptable risk
Disclose AI use and provide human oversight for high-risk applications

impact_assessment.detail: High-risk AI systems must undergo conformity assessment before deployment; operators must register systems in national AI registry

prohibited_categories.detail: Defines unacceptable-risk AI systems prohibited outright, including social scoring, behavioral manipulation, real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, and systems exploiting vulnerabilities

human_review_rights.detail: Human oversight and intervention rights required for high-risk AI systems in consequential decision-making contexts

private_right_of_action.detail: Executive regulation implementing Law 31814; enforcement is administrative through INDECOPI and sector regulators.

synthetic_media.detail: Implementing regulation for AI governance framework; synthetic media addressed through separate digital communications rules.

biometric_data.detail: No specific biometric provisions; addressed under Peru's data protection framework.

training_data_transparency.detail: AI system providers must submit technical documentation including training data summaries to the competent regulator.

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling provisions in this implementing regulation.

anti_discrimination.detail: Non-discrimination in AI deployment required; enforcement defers to existing equality and civil rights frameworks rather than creating new standards

risk_classification.detail: Four-tier risk framework (minimal, limited, high, unacceptable) modeled on EU AI Act; high-risk systems subject to pre-deployment conformity assessment and registry

enforcement_model.detail: INDECOPI and sector ministries enforce with graduated administrative fines; criminal referral for serious violations.

full_name: Ley Federal de Proteccion de Datos Personales en Posesion de los Particulares (2025 revision)
enforcement_body: INAI (Instituto Nacional de Transparencia, Acceso a la Informacion y Proteccion de Datos)
max_penalty: Up to 5% of annual revenue
summary: Mexico's 2025 comprehensive revision of its data protection framework, replacing the 2010 LFPDPPP. Introduces AI-specific provisions including: mandatory disclosure of AI and automated decision-making in privacy notices, algorithmic logic transparency requirements, right to object to automated decision-making for high-risk decisions, human-in-the-loop requirements, and data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing including AI profiling.
notable: First major overhaul of Mexico's data protection framework since 2010; introduces GDPR-style automated decision-making rights and AI-specific transparency obligations separate from the labor-focused AI voice/image law.
legal_citation: LFPDPPP (2025 revision), Diario Oficial de la Federacion (March 2025)
key_obligations: Disclose AI and automated decision-making use in privacy notices
Provide algorithmic logic transparency to data subjects
Implement human-in-the-loop for high-risk automated decisions
Allow individuals to object to automated decision-making
Conduct data protection impact assessments for AI profiling

impact_assessment.detail: Data Protection Impact Assessment required for AI profiling and high-risk automated processing of personal data

prohibited_categories.detail: Data protection amendment; no AI-specific prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Right to object to automated decisions for high-risk processing; human-in-the-loop required for decisions with significant legal or similar effects

private_right_of_action.detail: Data subjects may seek damages and injunctive relief through INAI or civil courts for violations of their data rights.

synthetic_media.detail: Data protection amendment; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data classified as sensitive requiring explicit consent; disclosure of AI processing in privacy notices is mandatory

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data transparency requirements; focuses on consent and lawful basis for data processing.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory automated processing prohibited under existing Mexican equality laws; data protection amendment defers to those frameworks.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification system; data protection obligations tied to data sensitivity categories.

enforcement_model.detail: INAI can impose fines up to 5% of annual revenue; INAI enforcement has addressed AI and automated profiling cases under the prior LFPDPPP

full_name: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026
enforcement_body: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
max_penalty: Administrative fine: up to INR 250 crore (~$30,000,000) for significant intermediaries; INR 50 lakh (~$60,000) for others
summary: Amends India's IT Intermediary Guidelines to regulate Synthetically Generated Information (SGI — the Indian legal term for AI-generated content). Requires platforms to label AI-generated audio, video, and images with a mandatory metadata identifier visible across at least 10% of the display area. Platforms must remove unlabeled synthetic content within three hours of notice. Defines SGI broadly to cover deepfakes, voice cloning, and AI-generated text in certain contexts.
notable: India's first binding deepfake and AI content labeling rule; three-hour takedown window is one of the world's fastest platform removal obligations for synthetic media.
legal_citation: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules 2026, MeitY Gazette Notification (Feb 2026)
key_obligations: Label AI-generated content with metadata identifier covering 10% of display area
Remove unlabeled synthetic content within three hours of notice
Maintain audit logs of synthetic content removal actions
Apply SGI labeling to audio, video, images, and specified text content
Notify users when AI-generated content is served to them

impact_assessment.detail: IT Rules amendment focuses on platform AI disclosure obligations; does not require impact assessments.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI categories; imposes disclosure and due diligence obligations on intermediaries deploying AI.

human_review_rights.detail: Users must be informed when AI is used in significant platform decisions; explanation provided but no formal right to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement through Ministry of Electronics and IT grievance mechanisms; no private right of action against platforms.

synthetic_media.detail: Mandatory metadata identifier covering at least 10% of the display area for all AI-generated audio, video, and images; implicit technical marking also required

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under DPDPA separately; IT Rules focus on platform AI governance.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data requirements; focuses on deployment-stage disclosure obligations.

content_labeling.detail: All AI-generated audio-visual content must carry SGI label; platforms must remove unlabeled synthetic content within three hours of notice — one of the fastest takedown mandates globally

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination standard; defers to existing Indian equality frameworks.

risk_classification.detail: No formal risk classification; obligations apply to all significant AI-driven platform decisions.

enforcement_model.detail: Three-hour platform removal obligation with escalating penalties for non-compliance; MeitY can direct ISP-level blocking for systematic failures

full_name: Decision of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress on Amending the Cybersecurity Law of the People's Republic of China
max_penalty: Up to RMB 10 million (~USD 1.4M)
summary: First major amendment to China's Cybersecurity Law since its 2017 enactment. Adds explicit AI safety provisions: AI systems deployed in critical infrastructure and key sectors must meet cybersecurity standards, AI providers must conduct security assessments, and entities using AI must implement AI ethics standards and monitoring. Increases maximum fines tenfold (from RMB 1M to RMB 10M) and adds personal liability for responsible persons.
notable: First formal AI-specific obligations under China's cybersecurity legal framework; significantly increases penalties applicable to AI providers in critical sectors.
legal_citation: Decision of the SCNPC Amending the Cybersecurity Law, NPC Order (Oct 2025)
key_obligations: AI in critical infrastructure must meet CAC cybersecurity standards
Conduct AI security assessments before deployment in key sectors
Implement AI ethics standards and ongoing monitoring
Report AI-related cybersecurity incidents to authorities
Designated responsible persons subject to personal liability for violations

impact_assessment.detail: AI systems in critical information infrastructure and key sectors must undergo security assessments before deployment; assessments must be repeated after significant model changes

prohibited_categories.detail: AI applications that threaten national security, undermine social stability, or facilitate circumvention of cyber sovereignty measures are prohibited.

human_review_rights.detail: Cybersecurity amendment focuses on infrastructure protection; no individual human review rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative enforcement through CAC, MIIT, and MPS; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Cybersecurity law amendments focus on network security and data protection; synthetic media addressed under Deep Synthesis regulation.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under PIPL; cybersecurity amendments focus on network-level security.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; focuses on data security and cross-border data transfer.

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling requirements; addressed under GenAI and AI Labelling Measures separately.

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination provisions; cybersecurity framework is infrastructure-focused.

risk_classification.detail: AI systems in critical sectors face enhanced security tier obligations; national-level AI safety standards become binding through cybersecurity law framework

enforcement_model.detail: CAC and MPS enforcement; fines up to RMB 10 million and personal liability for responsible persons; tenfold increase over pre-amendment maximum

full_name: Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024 (Ethiopia)
max_penalty: Administrative penalty: up to ETB 2,000,000 (~$35,000); criminal referral for wilful violations
summary: Ethiopia's foundational personal data protection law, modeled on the GDPR. AI-relevant provisions include: right to object to automated decision-making affecting individuals' legal interests, data protection impact assessments required for high-risk processing including AI profiling, explicit consent required for biometric data processing, and the right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects.
notable: First comprehensive data protection law in Ethiopia; establishes Africa's largest-population data protection authority and includes automated decision-making rights applicable to AI systems.
legal_citation: Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024, Federal Negarit Gazette
key_obligations: Obtain explicit consent for processing biometric and sensitive personal data
Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk AI processing
Allow individuals to object to purely automated decisions with significant effects
Appoint a Data Protection Officer for systematic high-risk processing
Register with the Ethiopian Personal Data Protection Commission

impact_assessment.detail: Data Protection Impact Assessment required for systematic processing of sensitive data including AI profiling of natural persons

prohibited_categories.detail: Data protection proclamation; no AI-specific prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with significant effects; data subject may request human review and the controller must reconsider

private_right_of_action.detail: Data subjects may claim compensation for damages; enforcement through Ethiopian Data Protection Authority and civil courts.

synthetic_media.detail: Data protection framework; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric, genetic, and health data classified as sensitive requiring explicit consent; special safeguards apply to AI processing of these categories

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; focuses on consent and lawful basis for processing existing personal data.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory automated processing not explicitly addressed; defers to Ethiopian constitution and equality laws.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; data protection obligations based on data sensitivity.

enforcement_model.detail: Ethiopian Personal Data Protection Commission enforces; penalty quantum to be set by regulation; Commission has investigative and corrective order powers

full_name: Law 2502 of 2025 — AI-Facilitated Identity Fraud Criminal Aggravator
enforcement_body: Fiscalia General de la Nacion (Prosecutor General)
max_penalty: Criminal penalties increased by up to one-third
summary: Amends Colombia's Criminal Code to classify the use of AI in identity fraud (deepfakes, digital voice/image impersonation) as a specific criminal aggravating circumstance, increasing applicable prison sentences by up to one-third. Covers AI-enabled identity theft, fraudulent impersonation using synthetic media, and unauthorized use of a person's digital likeness.
notable: One of the first laws in Latin America to specifically criminalize AI-enabled identity fraud; targets deepfake impersonation as an aggravated offense.
legal_citation: Law 2502 of 2025, Diario Oficial de Colombia
key_obligations: Prohibition on using AI to fraudulently impersonate individuals
Criminal penalty enhancement (up to one-third longer sentences) for AI-facilitated identity crimes
Covers deepfake video, synthetic voice, and digital likeness misuse

impact_assessment.detail: Criminal law aggravator; no impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: AI-facilitated identity fraud and digital impersonation classified as criminally aggravated offenses; effectively prohibits certain AI-enabled deception as a matter of criminal law

human_review_rights.detail: Criminal law framework; no civil human review rights provisions.

private_right_of_action.detail: Victims may bring civil claims alongside criminal proceedings; aggravated AI crimes enable enhanced civil damages.

synthetic_media.detail: Criminal aggravating circumstance for using AI (deepfakes, synthetic voice/image) in identity crimes; increases penalties by up to one-third

biometric_data.detail: Criminal aggravator applies broadly; biometric-specific crimes addressed under separate Colombian data protection law.

training_data_transparency.detail: Criminal law; no training data provisions.

anti_discrimination.detail: AI-aggravated discriminatory crimes prosecuted under existing Colombian criminal equality provisions.

risk_classification.detail: Criminal aggravation based on AI use in commission of offence, not a risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal penalties increased by one-third for AI-facilitated identity crimes; prosecution by Fiscalia General; no dedicated civil remedy

short_name: Brazil AI Crimes Against Women Law
full_name: Lei No. 15,123 de 2025 — Protection Against AI-Enabled Crimes Against Women
max_penalty: Up to 8 years imprisonment
summary: Criminalizes the creation, distribution, or use of AI-generated deepfakes and synthetic media to harass, intimidate, or commit crimes against women. Imposes criminal penalties of up to 8 years imprisonment for creating or sharing non-consensual AI-generated intimate images targeting women. Platforms must remove flagged content within 24 hours. Signed by President Lula in response to high-profile deepfake abuse cases.
notable: Brazil's first AI-specific criminal law; targets gender-based AI harms and deepfake abuse; 24-hour takedown obligation for platforms is one of the fastest in the Americas.
legal_citation: Lei No. 15.123, de 24 de abril de 2025, Diario Oficial da Uniao
key_obligations: Prohibition on creating or distributing non-consensual AI-generated intimate imagery targeting women
Platforms must remove flagged deepfake content within 24 hours
Criminal penalties up to 8 years imprisonment for AI-enabled gender-based crimes
Victim right of action for civil damages

impact_assessment.detail: Criminal law targeting AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery; no impact assessment requirements.

prohibited_categories.detail: Creates specific criminal offenses for AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and AI-enabled crimes against women; prohibits conduct rather than systems

human_review_rights.detail: Criminal law; no civil human review rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Victims may bring civil actions for actual damages, moral damages, and injunctions for content removal against perpetrators and platforms

synthetic_media.detail: Criminal penalties up to 8 years plus civil damages for non-consensual AI-generated intimate images; platforms must remove content within 24 hours

biometric_data.detail: Addresses AI-generated intimate imagery; biometric data addressed under LGPD separately.

training_data_transparency.detail: Criminal law; no training data provisions.

content_labeling.detail: Prohibits rather than labels the content in question.

anti_discrimination.detail: Targets gender-based AI crimes; defers to Brazil's Maria da Penha Law and constitutional equality frameworks.

risk_classification.detail: Criminal law; targeted prohibition rather than risk classification.

enforcement_model.detail: Criminal penalties up to 8 years imprisonment plus civil damages; 24-hour platform takedown obligation; Delegacia de Defesa da Mulher has primary criminal jurisdiction

short_name: Russia Moscow AI Experimental Legal Regime
full_name: Federal Law No. 123-FZ on Experimental Legal Regimes in the Field of Digital Innovation in Moscow
max_penalty: None — Experimental sandbox regime; general civil law applies. No specific AI penalty.
preemption_notes: Participants in the sandbox are exempt from specified provisions of general laws
summary: Russia's experimental legal regime framework for AI innovation in Moscow. Grants participating companies waivers from specified general laws (data protection, transport, medical) to develop AI, autonomous vehicles, medical diagnostics, and fintech applications. Establishes a regulatory sandbox with oversight by the Ministry of Economic Development and sector regulators. Participants must disclose AI use and conduct safety assessments for high-risk deployments. The sandbox model has expanded to additional sectors and cities.
notable: Russia's primary AI governance instrument; no comprehensive national AI law exists. Prioritises innovation and state control over rights-based protections. Biometric digital profiles enabled under this law raised significant civil society concern.
legal_citation: Federal Law No. 123-FZ, Rossiiskaya Gazeta (Aug 2020)
key_obligations: Participants must obtain sandbox designation from Ministry of Economic Development
Disclose AI use to users in participating deployments
Conduct safety assessments for high-risk AI applications
Submit periodic compliance reports to oversight authority
Maintain participant status — violations result in sandbox exclusion and reinstatement of general law obligations

impact_assessment.detail: Safety assessments required for participants deploying AI in transport, healthcare, or financial services sectors under the sandbox regime

prohibited_categories.detail: Experimental legal regime is permissive/sandbox by design; no prohibited AI categories within the experiment zone.

human_review_rights.detail: Experimental sandbox; human review rights not established within the regime.

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative sandbox regime; civil liability for AI harms addressed under general Russian civil law.

synthetic_media.detail: Experimental regime focuses on AI deployment in Moscow; synthetic media not specifically addressed.

biometric_data.detail: Moscow experiment permitted facial recognition in transport; biometric data rules embedded in experiment terms, not a general standard.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data transparency requirements within the experimental regime.

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination standard within the experimental regime.

risk_classification.detail: Sandbox/experimental regime; no formal risk classification system.

enforcement_model.detail: Sandbox exclusion is primary sanction; no dedicated penalty regime for AI harms — general civil and criminal law applies

full_name: Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Pakistan)
enforcement_body: National Commission for Personal Data Protection (NCPDP)
max_penalty: Up to PKR 25 million (~USD 90K) for serious violations
summary: Pakistan's first comprehensive data protection law, establishing rights over personal data processing. AI-relevant provisions include: right to object to automated decision-making with legal or significant effects, data protection impact assessments required for high-risk processing including AI profiling, biometric and health data classified as sensitive requiring explicit consent, and rights of access, rectification, and erasure applicable to AI-processed data.
notable: First data protection law covering Pakistan's 230 million population; GDPR-influenced ADM rights apply to AI systems; NCPDP still being established as of 2025.
legal_citation: Personal Data Protection Act 2023, Pakistan Gazette Extraordinary (Oct 2023)
key_obligations: Obtain explicit consent for processing sensitive personal data including biometrics
Conduct data protection impact assessments for high-risk AI processing
Provide right to object to automated decisions with significant effects
Register high-risk processing with NCPDP
Appoint Data Protection Officer for systematic high-risk processing

impact_assessment.detail: DPIA required for high-risk processing including systematic profiling and automated decision-making affecting individuals' legal or significant interests

prohibited_categories.detail: Data protection act; no AI-specific prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals can object to automated decisions with significant effects; controllers must carry out human review on request

private_right_of_action.detail: Data subjects may seek compensation and injunctive relief through the Personal Data Protection Authority and courts.

synthetic_media.detail: Data protection framework; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric, genetic, and health data are sensitive categories requiring explicit consent; heightened protections apply to AI processing of these categories

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; focuses on consent and lawful processing of personal data.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory data processing prohibited indirectly; defers to Pakistan's existing constitutional equality protections.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; data protection obligations based on data sensitivity categories.

enforcement_model.detail: NCPDP can impose fines up to PKR 25M (~USD 90K) for serious violations; injunctions and corrective orders also available

short_name: Qatar Personal Data Privacy Protection Law
full_name: Law No. 13 of 2016 on the Protection of Personal Data Privacy
max_penalty: Up to QAR 5 million (~USD 1.37M) and imprisonment
summary: Qatar's personal data protection law establishing rights and obligations for personal data processing. Applied to AI systems through NCSA guidance. Requires consent for processing personal data, provides access and rectification rights, and classifies sensitive data (health, biometric, financial) with heightened protections. Penalties include both fines and imprisonment for serious violations.
notable: Among the higher-penalty data protection regimes in the Gulf; imprisonment provisions create criminal liability for serious data protection violations including those arising from AI systems.
legal_citation: Law No. 13 of 2016, Qatar Official Gazette
key_obligations: Obtain consent for collection and processing of personal data
Provide data subjects with access, rectification, and deletion rights
Apply heightened protections to sensitive data including biometrics and health data
Register personal data processing operations with NCSA
Implement technical and organisational measures for data security

impact_assessment.detail: Controllers processing sensitive data (including biometrics, health, financial) must conduct privacy impact assessments under MOCI oversight.

prohibited_categories.detail: Data protection law; no AI-specific prohibited categories.

human_review_rights.detail: Data subjects have rights to access and rectification of personal data; explanation of processing logic available but no explicit AI review right.

private_right_of_action.detail: Civil compensation claims available for PDPPL violations; MOCI handles complaints with referral to Qatari courts.

synthetic_media.detail: Data protection law; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric and health data classified as sensitive requiring specific consent; heightened protections apply

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; 2016 law predates ML training data concerns.

anti_discrimination.detail: No explicit anti-discrimination standard in data processing context.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework; obligations based on data sensitivity and cross-border transfer.

enforcement_model.detail: NCSA enforces with fines up to QAR 5M (~USD 1.37M) plus criminal imprisonment for aggravated violations

full_name: Amendments to the Law on Informatization and Law on Personal Data relating to Artificial Intelligence (Uzbekistan)
enforcement_body: Agency for Development of Electronic Government
max_penalty: None — Development framework amendment; no published penalty schedule.
summary: Uzbekistan's AI governance amendments establish the first Central Asian AI framework alongside Kazakhstan's 2025 AI Law. Introduces AI-specific provisions into the Law on Informatization: risk-based classification for AI systems, mandatory impact assessments before public sector deployment, disclosure requirements when AI is used in decisions affecting citizens, and human review rights for high-impact automated decisions. Establishes an AI ethics framework for government AI deployments.
notable: One of the first AI governance instruments in Central Asia; predates Kazakhstan's 2025 AI Law by 18 months; focuses primarily on public sector AI with limited private sector obligations.
legal_citation: Amendments to Law on Informatization, Uzbekistan National Legislation Database (2024)
key_obligations: Classify AI systems by risk level before public sector deployment
Conduct impact assessments for high-risk AI in government decision-making
Disclose AI use to citizens affected by automated government decisions
Provide human review for high-impact automated decisions in public services
Register AI systems used in public services with Ministry of Digital Technologies

impact_assessment.detail: Impact assessments required before deployment of AI systems in public sector decision-making

prohibited_categories.detail: AI development framework amendment; no prohibited AI categories defined.

human_review_rights.detail: Citizens may request human review of automated government decisions; review must be completed within prescribed timeframe

private_right_of_action.detail: State-directed enforcement through Ministry of Digital Technologies; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: AI development law; does not specifically address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: AI framework amendment; biometric data addressed under Uzbekistan's separate personal data law.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data transparency requirements in this development-focused amendment.

risk_classification.detail: Risk classification distinguishes high-impact public sector AI (mandatory assessment and disclosure) from lower-risk systems

enforcement_model.detail: Ministry-level oversight without published penalty schedule; enforcement model not comparable to penalty-based systems.

full_name: OECD Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: None — Non-binding voluntary recommendation; no penalty mechanism.
preemption_notes: Non-binding recommendation; adopted by 46+ countries. Referenced in national AI laws across the EU, Asia-Pacific, and Americas.
summary: The OECD AI Principles are the first intergovernmental standard on AI, adopted by 46 countries. They establish five values-based principles: inclusive growth and sustainable development; human-centred values and fairness; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability. Updated in 2024 to address generative AI and agentic systems.
notable: Referenced in the preambles of the EU AI Act, UK AI White Paper, G7 Hiroshima Process, and domestic AI laws in over 40 countries.
legal_citation: OECD/LEGAL/0449
key_obligations: AI must respect rule of law and human rights
AI systems must be explainable
Actors must be accountable for AI outcomes
AI must be robust and secure throughout lifecycle

impact_assessment.detail: Recommends risk assessment before deployment; non-binding but adopted as standard by implementing countries.

prohibited_categories.detail: Principles-based framework; does not define prohibited AI applications.

human_review_rights.detail: Principle 1.3 requires meaningful human oversight for AI systems affecting individuals.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary framework; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media specifically; 2024 update notes generative AI risks generally.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions.

training_data_transparency.detail: Transparency principle applies generally but no training data disclosure requirement.

anti_discrimination.detail: Principle 1.2 requires AI to respect human rights and non-discrimination; defers to national frameworks.

risk_classification.detail: No formal risk classification; risk-based approach recommended but not mandated.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding recommendation; enforcement left entirely to member states.

full_name: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: None — Non-binding recommendation adopted by 193 states; no enforcement mechanism.
preemption_notes: Adopted by all 193 UNESCO member states. Non-binding but the broadest consensus instrument on AI ethics globally. Has influenced national AI strategies in Africa, Latin America, and Asia-Pacific.
summary: Adopted unanimously by 193 UNESCO member states, this Recommendation is the broadest global consensus instrument on AI ethics. It covers human rights, sustainability, peace, privacy, fairness, transparency, accountability, and the environment. It includes a Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM) to help member states evaluate their AI governance capacity.
notable: First global normative instrument on AI ethics adopted by all 193 UNESCO member states; includes the Readiness Assessment Methodology (RAM) used by 50+ countries.
legal_citation: UNESCO SHS/BIO/PIIC/2021/3
key_obligations: Member states should conduct readiness assessments
AI must respect human dignity and rights
Gender equality and non-discrimination must be ensured
Environmental impact of AI must be assessed
Moratorium on high-risk AI applications recommended pending robust safeguards

impact_assessment.detail: Recommends AI ethics impact assessments before deployment; includes Readiness Assessment Methodology for states.

prohibited_categories.detail: Recommends moratorium on high-risk applications (e.g., real-time biometric surveillance) but does not formally prohibit.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals should have the right to contest significant AI decisions affecting them.

private_right_of_action.detail: Non-binding recommendation; no enforcement or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not specifically address synthetic media or deepfakes.

biometric_data.detail: Recommends moratorium on real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces pending adequate safeguards.

training_data_transparency.detail: Transparency principle covers outputs but not training data specifically.

anti_discrimination.detail: Requires impact assessments to identify and mitigate discriminatory outcomes; impact-based standard.

risk_classification.detail: Recommends risk-based approach; states to develop own classification schemes aligned with Recommendation principles.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding; implementation through national AI strategies and RAM assessments; no penalty mechanism.

short_name: G7 Hiroshima AI Code of Conduct
full_name: G7 Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems
max_penalty: None — Voluntary industry code of conduct; no penalty mechanism.
preemption_notes: Voluntary industry code of conduct agreed by G7 leaders (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, UK, US, EU). Directly influenced Japanese AI Promotion Act and EU GPAI Code of Practice.
summary: The G7 Hiroshima Process Code of Conduct, agreed by G7 leaders in October 2023 under Japan's G7 presidency, establishes 11 voluntary principles for advanced AI developers. It covers transparency, safety, security, content authentication, reporting incidents, cybersecurity, and trustworthy AI. It was the first major international agreement specifically targeting frontier AI systems.
notable: First G7 agreement specifically targeting frontier AI; directly shaped the EU GPAI Code of Practice and Japan's AI Promotion Act.
legal_citation: G7 Hiroshima AI Process (2023)
key_obligations: Identify and mitigate risks throughout AI lifecycle
Report AI incidents to governments
Implement content authentication (watermarking)
Prioritise safety and security in AI development
Publish transparency reports

impact_assessment.detail: Principle 1 requires developers to identify and mitigate risks; safety evaluations required before and after deployment of frontier models.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary code; no prohibited categories defined.

human_review_rights.detail: Code targets developers; no individual human review rights created.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary code; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Principle 8 requires implementation of technical mechanisms (watermarking) to enable identification of AI-generated content.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions in the Code.

training_data_transparency.detail: Principle 5 requires sharing information with governments on AI capabilities, training data sources, and risk evaluations.

content_labeling.detail: Watermarking and content provenance mechanisms required; disclosure to users of AI-generated content.

anti_discrimination.detail: No explicit anti-discrimination provisions; fairness addressed through general risk mitigation principle.

risk_classification.detail: Applies to 'advanced AI systems'; no formal risk tier classification scheme.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary code; no penalty regime. G7 tasked OECD with monitoring adoption.

full_name: UN General Assembly Resolution A/78/265: Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy artificial intelligence systems for sustainable development
max_penalty: None — Non-binding UN GA resolution; no enforcement mechanism.
preemption_notes: Non-binding UN General Assembly resolution adopted by consensus of 193 member states. Politically significant as first UN-level consensus on AI governance.
summary: The first UN General Assembly resolution on AI governance, adopted by consensus in March 2024. It calls on member states to develop safe, secure, and trustworthy AI; emphasises the need to bridge the digital divide; highlights AI risks to human rights; and requests the Secretary-General to establish a High-Level Advisory Body on AI.
notable: First UN General Assembly consensus on AI; US co-sponsored with 120+ co-sponsors; establishes the High-Level AI Advisory Body (AIAB).
key_obligations: States to promote safe, secure, trustworthy AI for SDGs
Bridge the AI divide between developed and developing nations
Respect human rights in AI development and use
Support the UN Secretary-General's AI governance initiatives

impact_assessment.detail: Resolution encourages responsible AI; does not mandate specific impact assessment procedures.

prohibited_categories.detail: Does not define prohibited AI uses.

human_review_rights.detail: References human rights generally; no specific human review right created.

private_right_of_action.detail: UN resolution; no enforcement mechanism or private right.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media specifically.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions.

anti_discrimination.detail: Resolution emphasises human rights and non-discrimination; defers to existing international human rights framework.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework.

enforcement_model.detail: Non-binding political resolution; no penalty mechanism.

full_name: NIST Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
max_penalty: None — Voluntary framework; compliance is self-assessed. No penalty.
preemption_notes: Voluntary framework for private sector; referenced as standard in federal procurement. Some agencies and states cite NIST AI RMF compliance as a safe harbour factor.
summary: Published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the AI RMF provides a structured approach to managing AI risks through four core functions: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, and MANAGE. It is voluntary for private industry but referenced in federal contracting requirements and cited in state AI bills. It is accompanied by the AI RMF Playbook with specific recommended actions.
notable: The dominant US private-sector AI risk management standard; referenced in Colorado SB 205, Texas TRAIGA, and over 30 state AI bills as a compliance benchmark.
legal_citation: NIST AI 100-1
key_obligations: Establish AI governance policies (GOVERN)
Identify AI risks in context (MAP)
Analyse and prioritise AI risks (MEASURE)
Address and monitor AI risks (MANAGE)
Document AI system capabilities and limitations

impact_assessment.detail: MEASURE function requires systematic risk assessment; MAP function identifies context-specific harms before deployment.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary framework; no prohibited categories — risk management approach instead.

human_review_rights.detail: Framework is organisational; does not create individual rights to human review.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary framework; no enforcement mechanism or private right.

synthetic_media.detail: Generative AI profile (NIST AI 600-1) addresses deepfake risks but does not mandate labeling.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions in core framework.

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling requirements; content authenticity addressed in Generative AI Profile.

risk_classification.detail: MAP function requires classification of AI use cases by risk level; higher risk applications require more rigorous treatment.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary framework; compliance is self-assessed. Federal procurement increasingly references alignment as evaluation criterion.

operative_dates: Published Jan 2023. Living document; Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) released Jul 2024 as supplementary guidance.

full_name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS)
max_penalty: None — Voluntary standard; certification is optional. No regulatory penalty.

synthetic_media.detail: No synthetic media specific requirements.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific controls; general data governance applies.

full_name: ISO/IEC 23894:2023 — Information Technology: Artificial Intelligence — Guidance on Risk Management

Analyse and evaluate AI risks in context
Implement risk treatment measures
Monitor AI risks continuously

human_review_rights.detail: Does not create individual rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary standard; no enforcement.

synthetic_media.detail: No synthetic media provisions.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions.

training_data_transparency.detail: Data quality as a risk source identified; no disclosure requirement.

anti_discrimination.detail: Bias identified as risk source; no formal discrimination standard.

risk_classification.detail: Risk level determines treatment intensity; higher-risk AI requires more comprehensive treatment measures.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary guidance; no penalty mechanism.

short_name: EU AI Office Guidelines on Prohibited Practices
full_name: EU AI Office Guidelines on Prohibited AI Practices (Article 5 EU AI Act)
max_penalty: €35,000,000 or 7% global turnover (per parent EU AI Act)
preemption_notes: Authoritative interpretation of EU AI Act Article 5 prohibited practices. Directly applicable guidance; member state authorities must apply it from 2 February 2025.
summary: Published by the EU AI Office on 4 February 2025, these guidelines provide authoritative interpretation of the eight categories of prohibited AI practices under Article 5 of the EU AI Act. legal_citation: EU AI Office Guidelines (Art. 5 EU AI Act)
key_obligations: Ban on subliminal manipulation causing harm
Ban on exploitation of vulnerabilities
Ban on public authority social scoring
Ban on real-time biometric surveillance with limited exceptions
Ban on emotion recognition in workplace and education
Ban on biometric categorisation from internet scraping

human_review_rights.detail: Guidelines focus on prohibited practices; human oversight addressed in high-risk AI provisions separately.

private_right_of_action.detail: Enforcement is administrative by national market surveillance authorities; private action follows national procedural law.
