biometric_data.detail: Guidelines interpret the prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces, including the narrow law enforcement exceptions.

training_data_transparency.detail: Not addressed in prohibited practices context.

content_labeling.detail: Content labeling is a transparency provision, not a prohibition.

anti_discrimination.detail: Guidelines explicitly link prohibited practices to fundamental rights; biometric categorisation prohibition grounded in anti-discrimination principle.

risk_classification.detail: These are the unacceptable risk (prohibited) tier of the EU AI Act four-tier system; guidelines do not address the broader classification framework.

enforcement_model.detail: Violations of prohibited practices carry the highest EU AI Act penalties: €35M or 7% global turnover. EU AI Office and national market surveillance authorities enforce.

operative_dates: Guidelines issued Feb 2025 on the prohibited AI practices provisions of the EU AI Act, which became applicable 2 Feb 2025.

full_name: EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice — First Draft (EU AI Act Articles 53–55)
max_penalty: €15,000,000 or 3% global turnover (per EU AI Act Art. 101 for GPAI)
preemption_notes: Developed under EU AI Act Art. 56 multi-stakeholder process. Compliance creates a presumption of conformity with GPAI obligations. Final version expected mid-2025.
summary: Developed through a multi-stakeholder process convened by the EU AI Office under Article 56 of the EU AI Act, this Code of Practice sets out the specific obligations for General-Purpose AI (GPAI) model providers. It covers transparency, training data copyright compliance, systemic risk assessment, cybersecurity, and content watermarking for frontier models. Compliance creates a presumption of conformity with the EU AI Act's GPAI provisions.
notable: First international compliance code specifically for frontier AI model providers; creates a presumption of conformity with EU AI Act GPAI chapter — effectively a safe harbour.
legal_citation: EU AI Act Art. 53–56
key_obligations: Publish technical documentation and model card
Copyright compliance policy for training data
Systemic risk assessment for high-capability models
Implement adversarial testing (red-teaming)
Watermark AI-generated content
Report serious incidents to EU AI Office

impact_assessment.detail: Systematic risk assessment and adversarial testing required before deployment of GPAI models above capability thresholds.

prohibited_categories.detail: Code addresses GPAI obligations; prohibited practices are covered in separate EU AI Act provisions.

human_review_rights.detail: GPAI Code does not create individual human review rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Code creates presumption of conformity; enforcement is by EU AI Office and national authorities.

synthetic_media.detail: GPAI providers must implement technical solutions to mark AI-generated content; watermarking standards to be specified by EU AI Office.

biometric_data.detail: GPAI Code does not address biometric data specifically.

training_data_transparency.detail: Training data summary (including copyright compliance policy) must be published; detailed documentation provided to EU AI Office on request.

content_labeling.detail: AI-generated content from GPAI models must be marked to enable detection; technical specifications issued by EU AI Office.

anti_discrimination.detail: GPAI Code focuses on systemic risks; anti-discrimination for applications is addressed under high-risk provisions.

risk_classification.detail: GPAI models classified by capability threshold (training compute ≥ 10²⁵ FLOPs = systemic risk); higher tier faces additional requirements.

enforcement_model.detail: EU AI Office enforces GPAI obligations directly; penalties up to €15M or 3% global turnover; Code compliance creates safe harbour presumption.

implementation_phases.description: GPAI model transparency obligations under EU AI Act begin applying
First draft of GPAI Code of Practice published
GPAI systemic risk provisions and Code of Practice expected to be finalised

full_name: Argentine Artificial Intelligence National Plan — Decree 1182/2024
enforcement_body: Secretariat of Innovation, Science and Technology
max_penalty: None — Executive decree for government internal use; no penalty for private sector.
preemption_notes: Federal executive decree; applies to national public administration. Provincial AI rules may coexist under Argentina's federal system.
summary: Decree 1182/2024 establishes Argentina's National AI Plan and creates an AI Ethics Committee within the national public administration. It requires impact assessments for AI systems used in government decisions, adopts a risk-based approach aligned with OECD principles, and mandates transparency for AI systems affecting citizens. The decree applies to national executive branch agencies and sets principles for future legislation.
notable: First Latin American executive decree establishing a mandatory AI ethics framework for government; creates a precedent before any national AI legislation is enacted.
legal_citation: Decreto 1182/2024 — Plan Nacional de Inteligencia Artificial
key_obligations: Impact assessment for AI in government decisions
AI Ethics Committee review of high-risk applications
Transparency to citizens of AI use in public services
Adherence to OECD AI Principles in government procurement

impact_assessment.detail: Mandatory algorithmic impact assessment required for AI systems used in government decisions affecting citizens.

prohibited_categories.detail: Framework decree; does not define prohibited AI uses beyond general human rights constraints.

human_review_rights.detail: Citizens have right to request human review of significant government AI decisions under the decree.

private_right_of_action.detail: Government internal decree; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under Argentina's Personal Data Protection Law separately.

anti_discrimination.detail: Requires compliance with constitutional equality principles; defers to existing anti-discrimination framework.

risk_classification.detail: High-risk government AI uses require Ethics Committee review; binary classification applied within government context.

enforcement_model.detail: Internal government oversight by AI Ethics Committee; no penalty mechanism for private sector.

short_name: Canada Voluntary Code of Conduct on GenAI
full_name: Voluntary Code of Conduct on the Responsible Development and Management of Advanced Generative AI Systems
enforcement_body: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED)
max_penalty: None — Voluntary industry code; signatories self-report. No penalty.
preemption_notes: Voluntary industry code; Canada's AIDA (Artificial Intelligence and Data Act) Bill C-27 failed to pass before 2025 election call. This code is the operative federal AI governance instrument for the private sector pending legislation.
summary: Canada's Voluntary Code of Conduct on Generative AI was published by ISED in September 2023 as an interim governance instrument following the failure of Bill C-27 (AIDA). It applies to organisations developing and deploying advanced generative AI systems and covers: safety testing, fairness and bias assessment, transparency to users, content labeling, human oversight, and reporting of significant harms. Major Canadian tech companies and multinational AI labs signed the code.
notable: Operative federal AI governance instrument for Canada following AIDA's failure; signed by major AI companies including Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and major Canadian banks.
legal_citation: ISED Voluntary Code of Conduct on GenAI (2023)
key_obligations: Safety testing before deployment
Bias and fairness assessment
Transparency disclosures to users about AI use
Content labeling of AI-generated material
Human oversight mechanisms for high-stakes decisions
Reporting significant AI harms to ISED

impact_assessment.detail: Safety testing and bias/fairness assessment required before deploying advanced generative AI systems.

prohibited_categories.detail: Voluntary code; no prohibited categories defined.

human_review_rights.detail: Human oversight required for high-stakes decisions but no individual right to request review created.

private_right_of_action.detail: Voluntary code; no enforcement mechanism or private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Content labeling of AI-generated material required; technical implementation left to signatories.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions in the voluntary code.

training_data_transparency.detail: Signatories must maintain information on training data sources; sharing with ISED on request.

content_labeling.detail: Explicit requirement to label AI-generated content to users; technical standard not prescribed.

anti_discrimination.detail: Bias assessment required; reasonable care to prevent discriminatory outcomes standard applied.

risk_classification.detail: No formal risk classification framework; applies to 'advanced' generative AI without defining threshold.

enforcement_model.detail: Voluntary; signatories self-report to ISED; no penalty mechanism.

short_name: Switzerland FADP (Revised Federal Act on Data Protection)
full_name: Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (revDSG / nFADP) — AI Applicability
enforcement_body: Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)
preemption_notes: Switzerland is not an EU member state; FADP is an independent sovereign framework not subject to EU AI Act directly. Switzerland and EU have a data adequacy arrangement; FADP was substantially revised to align with GDPR to maintain adequacy.
summary: Switzerland's revised Federal Act on Data Protection (revDSG/nFADP), in force since September 2023, substantially aligns Swiss data protection with the GDPR. It is relevant to AI through: mandatory data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, a right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects, opt-out from automated profiling, transparency obligations for automated processing, and special category protections for biometric and genetic data.
notable: Non-EU European country with GDPR-equivalent framework; the only significant European AI-applicable law outside EU, UK, and Council of Europe frameworks.
key_obligations: Data protection impact assessment for high-risk processing
Right to opt out of automated profiling decisions
Transparency about automated decision-making
Explicit consent for sensitive data including biometrics
Data subject rights to access, rectification, and deletion

impact_assessment.detail: Art. 22 requires data protection impact assessment for high-risk automated processing; FDPIC must be consulted if risks cannot be mitigated.

prohibited_categories.detail: No AI-specific prohibited categories; general data protection principles constrain high-risk processing.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 21 provides right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects; controller must enable human review on request.

private_right_of_action.detail: Criminal sanctions apply to serious violations; civil remedies under Swiss civil law; no statutory private right of action equivalent to GDPR damages.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not specifically address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data classified as sensitive personal data requiring explicit consent or other lawful basis under Art. 5.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; focuses on processing of existing personal data.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory automated profiling restricted; defers to Swiss constitutional equality provisions.

risk_classification.detail: No formal AI risk classification; risk assessed through DPIA process on case-by-case basis.

enforcement_model.detail: Maximum CHF 250,000 (~USD 280,000) criminal fine for intentional violations; significantly lower than GDPR. FDPIC has investigatory but limited enforcement powers.

full_name: Ukraine Draft Law on Artificial Intelligence (No. 11175)
max_penalty: None — Draft law not yet enacted; no penalty schedule finalised.
preemption_notes: Pending draft legislation; Ukraine is an EU candidate country and draft closely mirrors EU AI Act framework as part of EU accession alignment obligations.
summary: Ukraine's Draft Law No. 11175 on Artificial Intelligence, registered in the Verkhovna Rada in March 2024, closely mirrors the EU AI Act framework as part of Ukraine's EU accession obligations. It establishes a risk-based classification system, impact assessment requirements for high-risk AI, prohibited AI practices, content labeling, and human oversight rights. Legislative progress has been slow due to the ongoing war.
notable: EU candidate country AI law closely tracking EU AI Act; unique context of wartime AI use (drone targeting, surveillance) creating pressure for both adoption and carve-outs.
legal_citation: Draft Law No. 11175 (Verkhovna Rada)
key_obligations: Risk-based AI classification aligned with EU AI Act
Impact assessments for high-risk AI systems
Prohibited AI practices (social scoring, subliminal manipulation)
Content labeling and transparency requirements
Human oversight for consequential AI decisions

impact_assessment.detail: Draft requires impact assessments for high-risk AI systems; assessment framework closely mirrors EU AI Act Annex VI.

prohibited_categories.detail: Draft prohibits social scoring, subliminal manipulation, real-time biometric surveillance in public — EU AI Act prohibited practices adopted wholesale.

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have right to human review of significant AI decisions; mirrors EU AI Act Art. 14 human oversight requirement.

private_right_of_action.detail: Draft provides for administrative enforcement; private action under general civil law.

synthetic_media.detail: Content labeling of AI-generated material required; similar to EU AI Act transparency provisions for synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Draft prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces (with national security exceptions — broader than EU given wartime context).

training_data_transparency.detail: Technical documentation including training data information to be filed with national supervisory authority.

content_labeling.detail: AI-generated content must be labeled; applies to text, images, audio, and video.

anti_discrimination.detail: Impact assessment must identify discriminatory risks; reasonable care to prevent disparate impact required.

risk_classification.detail: Four-tier risk framework (prohibited/high-risk/limited-risk/minimal-risk) mirroring EU AI Act adopted in draft.

enforcement_model.detail: Administrative penalties for violations; enforcement authority TBD pending final passage; levels not yet specified in draft.

implementation_phases.description: Draft Law No. 11175 registered in Verkhovna Rada
Expected first reading (delayed due to wartime priorities)

short_name: Serbia Personal Data Protection Law (AI Applicability)
full_name: Serbia Law on Personal Data Protection — Provisions Applicable to AI (Law No. 87/2018, updated 2023)
enforcement_body: Commissioner for Information of Public Importance and Personal Data Protection (Serbia)
max_penalty: RSD 2,000,000 (~USD 18,000) for legal entities
preemption_notes: Serbia is an EU candidate country; PDPL substantially mirrors GDPR as part of EU accession Chapter 10 obligations. Serbia is also a Council of Europe member and has ratified Convention 108+.
summary: Serbia's Law on Personal Data Protection (Law No. 87/2018), modelled closely on GDPR, provides the operative AI governance framework for Serbia pending specific AI legislation. It covers: data protection impact assessments for high-risk processing, right not to be subject to solely automated decisions, explicit consent for biometric data, and data subject access and rectification rights applicable to AI-processed data.
notable: Western Balkans EU accession candidate — GDPR-mirroring law provides interim AI governance; Serbia is on CoE Convention 108+ implementation path.
legal_citation: Zakon o zaštiti podataka o ličnosti, Sl. glasnik RS, br. 87/2018
key_obligations: Data protection impact assessment for high-risk automated processing
Right to opt out of solely automated decisions
Explicit consent for biometric data processing
Data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure)

impact_assessment.detail: Art. 54 requires DPIA for high-risk processing including systematic evaluation of individuals using automated means.

prohibited_categories.detail: No AI-specific prohibited categories; general data protection principles apply.

human_review_rights.detail: Art. 38 provides right not to be subject to solely automated decisions with legal effects; right to human review on request.

private_right_of_action.detail: Complaints to Commissioner; civil damages under Serbian tort law; no specific private AI right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Art. 17 classifies biometric data as special category requiring explicit consent.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data provisions; focuses on processing of existing personal data.

anti_discrimination.detail: Non-discrimination in data processing required; defers to Serbia's Law on Prohibition of Discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: No AI risk classification; DPIA triggered by processing risk, not AI risk level.

enforcement_model.detail: Maximum RSD 2M (~USD 18,000) fine for legal entities; significantly lower than GDPR. Commissioner has investigatory powers.

full_name: Tunisia National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2023–2025 and Digital Economy Framework
enforcement_body: Instance Nationale de Protection des Données Personnelles (INPDP)
max_penalty: None — National strategy document; no penalty mechanism.
preemption_notes: National strategy document; Tunisia's data protection authority (INPDP) applies the 2004 personal data protection law to AI processing. New AI-specific legislation under development.
summary: Tunisia's National AI Strategy 2023–2025 focuses on four pillars: AI for economic competitiveness, AI infrastructure development, AI skills and talent, and regulatory and ethical framework. The strategy commits Tunisia to developing AI-specific legislation by 2025, adopting the UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation, and strengthening the INPDP's capacity to regulate AI data processing.
notable: First Maghreb country with a formal national AI strategy; INPDP (data protection authority) is one of the most active African AI regulators.
legal_citation: Tunisia National AI Strategy 2023–2025
key_obligations: Develop AI-specific legislation by 2025
Implement UNESCO AI Ethics Recommendation
Build AI regulatory capacity at INPDP
Invest in AI infrastructure and skills

prohibited_categories.detail: Strategy does not define prohibited AI uses.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual rights established by the strategy document.

private_right_of_action.detail: Strategy only; no enforcement mechanism.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data addressed under 2004 data protection law separately.

anti_discrimination.detail: Strategy references fairness principles but creates no binding standard.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework established.

enforcement_model.detail: Strategy document only; enforcement through INPDP's existing data protection mandate.

short_name: Morocco CNDP AI Data Protection Guidance
full_name: Morocco Commission Nationale de Contrôle de la Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel — AI and Personal Data Guidelines
enforcement_body: CNDP (Commission Nationale de contrôle de la Protection des Données à caractère Personnel)
max_penalty: MAD 300,000 (~USD 30,000) under Law 09-08
preemption_notes: Guidance issued under Morocco's Law 09-08 on Personal Data Protection (2009). Morocco is developing comprehensive AI legislation separately.
summary: Morocco's CNDP issued guidelines in 2024 on the application of Law 09-08 to AI systems processing personal data. The guidelines address: lawful basis for AI training data collection, transparency obligations for automated processing, DPIA requirements for high-risk AI, right to human review of algorithmic decisions, and restrictions on biometric AI use. Morocco's CNDP is one of the most active data protection authorities in Africa and Francophone world.
notable: Morocco's CNDP is among the most active African AI regulators; guidance adopted as a model by several Francophone African nations.
legal_citation: CNDP Recommandations sur l'IA et la Protection des Données (2024)
key_obligations: Lawful basis required for AI training data collection
DPIA for high-risk automated processing
Transparency to individuals about automated decisions
Right to contest automated decisions affecting individual rights
Prior authorisation for biometric AI systems

human_review_rights.detail: Individuals have right to contest significant automated decisions under Law 09-08 as interpreted by CNDP guidance.

risk_classification.detail: No formal AI risk classification; risk assessed through DPIA process.

enforcement_model.detail: Maximum MAD 300,000 (~USD 30,000) under Law 09-08; CNDP issues warnings, injunctions, and can refer to courts.

full_name: Shanghai Municipality Regulations on the Promotion and Development of the Artificial Intelligence Industry
enforcement_body: Shanghai Municipal Commission of Economy and Information Technology (SMECIT)
max_penalty: None — Promotion ordinance; violations referred to national regulatory framework.

notable: First city-level comprehensive AI ordinance in China — a legislative model subsequently adopted by Beijing and other major municipalities.

Training data governance policy required
Disclosure when AI used in public-facing government services
Risk assessment for high-impact AI in critical sectors
Safe harbour for AI products certified under national standards

Training data compliance with national content standards

Real-name registration of users for high-risk GenAI services

human_review_rights.detail: Does not create individual human review rights.

private_right_of_action.detail: Administrative enforcement; no private right of action.

synthetic_media.detail: All AI-generated content must be labeled; stricter than national GenAI Measures requirement.

full_name: Guangdong Province Artificial Intelligence Industry Development Regulations
enforcement_body: Guangdong Provincial Department of Industry and Information Technology
max_penalty: None — Promotion ordinance; penalties deferred to national CAC/MIIT framework.
preemption_notes: Provincial ordinance complementary to national AI regulations. Guangdong (home to Tencent, Huawei, DJI) uses the ordinance to attract AI investment while aligning with national governance requirements.
summary: Guangdong's AI Industry Development Regulations, building on Shanghai's 2022 model, establish a provincial framework for AI development and governance. notable: Largest provincial GDP in China; Guangdong ordinance shapes AI regulation for Shenzhen, Guangzhou, and the Greater Bay Area tech ecosystem.

Training data governance policy required for AI enterprises

AI product registration for cross-border Greater Bay Area deployment

short_name: ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (2023)
full_name: ASEAN Guide on Artificial Intelligence Governance and Ethics (2nd Edition, 2023)

The 2nd edition adds a chapter on generative AI and updates guidance on foundation models. It is accompanied by case studies from Singapore, Indonesia, and Thailand.
notable: The primary AI governance reference for all 10 ASEAN member states; directly shaped Thailand AI Act, Vietnam AI Law, and Indonesia AI policy discussions.
legal_citation: ASEAN AI Governance Guide (2nd ed., 2023)
key_obligations: Transparency and explainability for significant AI decisions
Fairness and non-discrimination assessment
Human oversight mechanisms for high-stakes AI
Privacy and data governance aligned with national frameworks

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited categories; FTC uses case-by-case unfairness analysis.

human_review_rights.detail: FTC policy does not create individual rights; remedies through enforcement actions.

private_right_of_action.detail: FTC Act does not include a private right of action; consumers cannot sue directly.

synthetic_media.detail: Statement addresses deceptive AI claims broadly; synthetic media covered through deception analysis.

biometric_data.detail: FTC has taken action against biometric data misuse; opt-out and consent requirements inferred from unfairness analysis.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure requirement; unfair training data practices (scraping without consent) subject to Section 5.

content_labeling.detail: No content labeling mandate; deceptive unlabeled AI content subject to FTC deception analysis.

anti_discrimination.detail: Discriminatory algorithmic outcomes may constitute unfair practices under Section 5; impact-based analysis applied in enforcement.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; FTC uses context-specific unfairness/deception analysis.

enforcement_model.detail: FTC civil penalties up to $50,120/day/violation; injunctions; consent orders. Landmark AI enforcement actions include Amazon Alexa children's privacy and Rite Aid facial recognition.

short_name: CFPB Circular on AI in Credit Decisions
full_name: CFPB Circular 2023-03: Adverse Action Notification Requirements and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act in the Context of Artificial Intelligence
max_penalty: $50,000 per day for pattern-or-practice violations (ECOA)
preemption_notes: Federal circular; ECOA and Regulation B apply nationally and preempt less protective state credit rules. CFPB enforcement supplements OCC, Fed, and FDIC examination for regulated entities.
summary: CFPB Circular 2023-03 clarifies that lenders using AI or complex machine learning models in credit decisions must comply with ECOA adverse action notice requirements regardless of model complexity. Lenders cannot use model opacity as an excuse to avoid providing specific reasons for credit denials. Circular addresses "black box" AI and requires explanations that are meaningful to applicants.
notable: First US federal agency guidance prohibiting 'black box' credit AI; effectively mandates explainability for AI in lending regardless of model complexity.
legal_citation: CFPB Circular 2023-03; 15 U.S.C. 1691e (ECOA)
key_obligations: Specific adverse action reasons required for all AI credit denials
Model complexity is not an excuse for inadequate explanation
Explanations must be meaningful and specific to the applicant
Discriminatory AI credit decisions violate ECOA

impact_assessment.detail: Circular addresses adverse action explanation; no impact assessment requirement created.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI categories; existing ECOA protected class prohibitions apply.

human_review_rights.detail: Applicants have right to specific explanation for AI credit denial; human review not mandated but explanation requirement effectively requires review capacity.

private_right_of_action.detail: ECOA provides private right of action; actual damages, punitive damages up to $10,000, and attorney fees available.

synthetic_media.detail: Does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric provisions; credit context only.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; focuses on output explainability.

anti_discrimination.detail: ECOA disparate impact standard applies to AI credit models; lenders liable for discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; ECOA obligations apply to all credit AI regardless of model type.

enforcement_model.detail: CFPB civil penalties up to $50K/day; ECOA private right of action; state AGs may also enforce under Dodd-Frank.

short_name: EEOC Technical Assistance on AI in Employment
full_name: EEOC Technical Assistance: Selecting Employees and Applicants Using Artificial Intelligence and Other Automated Systems
max_penalty: Compensatory + punitive damages under Title VII (up to $300,000)
preemption_notes: Federal employment discrimination law; EEOC guidance applies nationally. State employment discrimination laws may provide additional protections. NYC LL144 (annual bias audit) operates alongside federal EEOC framework.
summary: The EEOC's Technical Assistance document clarifies that employers who use AI, algorithmic decision-making, or automated systems in employment decisions remain fully liable under Title VII, ADA, ADEA, and other employment discrimination statutes. The guidance confirms that: disparate impact liability applies to AI hiring tools, employers are responsible for their vendors' AI tools, the ADA reasonable accommodation requirement extends to AI assessment formats, and the 4/5ths adverse impact rule applies to AI screening.
notable: Establishes that US employers cannot outsource discrimination liability to AI vendors; employers are liable for discriminatory AI tools even if purchased from third parties.
legal_citation: EEOC Technical Assistance (May 2023); 42 U.S.C. 2000e (Title VII)
key_obligations: Employers liable for AI hiring tool discrimination regardless of vendor responsibility
4/5ths adverse impact rule applies to AI screening tools
ADA reasonable accommodation must extend to AI assessment formats
Disparate impact analysis required for AI selection procedures

impact_assessment.detail: No mandatory impact assessment; EEOC recommends but does not require pre-deployment adverse impact analysis.

prohibited_categories.detail: Existing Title VII prohibited classifications (race, sex, religion, national origin) apply to AI; no new AI-specific prohibitions.

human_review_rights.detail: No right to human review of AI employment decisions; EEOC focuses on outcome liability.

private_right_of_action.detail: Title VII, ADA, ADEA all provide private rights of action; compensatory and punitive damages up to $300,000; injunctive relief available.

synthetic_media.detail: Employment context only; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric-specific provisions beyond ADA accommodation for biometric assessments.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; emphasis on employment outcome compliance.

anti_discrimination.detail: Disparate impact liability under Title VII applies to AI selection procedures; 4/5ths rule is the operative standard.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification; all employment AI subject to same Title VII framework.

enforcement_model.detail: EEOC investigates, conciliates, and litigates; private right of action after EEOC charge; compensatory + punitive damages up to $300K.

short_name: FDA AI/ML Action Plan for Software as Medical Device
full_name: FDA Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML)-Based Software as a Medical Device Action Plan
enforcement_body: FDA Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH)
max_penalty: Per 21 U.S.C. 333 — up to $15,000 per violation for device violations
preemption_notes: Federal medical device regulation preempts state SaMD requirements. FDA regulatory jurisdiction over AI/ML Software as Medical Device is exclusive federal domain; state laws cannot impose additional premarket requirements.
summary: The FDA's AI/ML Action Plan for Software as Medical Device (SaMD) establishes the agency's regulatory approach to AI-enabled medical devices. It outlines five action areas: tailored regulatory framework for AI/ML-based SaMD, good machine learning practice standards, patient-centred approaches, algorithm transparency, and real-world performance monitoring. The Action Plan underpins FDA's pre-submission program for AI medical devices and is being updated through the Predetermined Change Control Plan (PCCP) pathway.
notable: Governs all AI in FDA-regulated medical devices; the primary reason AI diagnostic tools, surgical robots, and clinical decision support require FDA clearance or approval.
legal_citation: FDA AI/ML SaMD Action Plan (2021); 21 U.S.C. 360 (FDCA)
key_obligations: Premarket submission (510(k) or PMA) for AI/ML-based SaMD
Good Machine Learning Practice standards compliance
Algorithm transparency for clinical users
Post-market performance monitoring and adverse event reporting
Predetermined Change Control Plan for continuously learning algorithms

impact_assessment.detail: Premarket review is a mandatory assessment before marketing; FDA evaluates clinical validation, training data, and performance across subgroups.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited categories; risk classification determines pathway (exempt/510(k)/De Novo/PMA).

human_review_rights.detail: FDA requires human oversight for high-risk clinical decisions; purely autonomous AI diagnosis in life-threatening contexts requires PMA and human review safeguards.

private_right_of_action.detail: FDCA enforcement is FDA/DOJ; no private right of action under FDCA; medical malpractice claims available separately.

synthetic_media.detail: Medical device context; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: Biometric data used in medical AI devices subject to device-specific FDA requirements; not general biometric regulation.

training_data_transparency.detail: Training and validation data characteristics must be submitted in premarket applications; subgroup performance across demographics required.

content_labeling.detail: Device labeling (instructions for use) must disclose AI nature; not content labeling in the generative AI sense.

anti_discrimination.detail: FDA requires subgroup performance analysis to identify demographic disparities in AI device performance; impact-based standard.

risk_classification.detail: Three-class device risk framework applies to AI SaMD: Class I (exempt), II (510(k)), III (PMA); higher risk = more rigorous review.

enforcement_model.detail: FDA Warning Letters, consent decrees, injunctions, and criminal referrals for device violations; civil penalties up to $15K/violation.

short_name: SEC Proposed Rule on Conflicts of Interest in AI (2023)
full_name: SEC Proposed Rule: Conflicts of Interest Associated with the Use of Predictive Data Analytics by Broker-Dealers and Investment Advisers
max_penalty: Per Exchange Act — civil penalties, disgorgement, injunctions
preemption_notes: Federal securities regulation; SEC rules preempt state securities laws for broker-dealers and registered investment advisers. Rule proposed under Exchange Act Section 15(l) and Advisers Act Section 211.
summary: The SEC's proposed rule would require broker-dealers and investment advisers to evaluate and eliminate or neutralise conflicts of interest when using predictive data analytics (including AI and ML) in investor interactions. The rule targets AI systems that optimise for firm interests at investors' expense. It requires: conflict identification through testing, documented conflict elimination or neutralisation, disclosure to investors, and compliance program requirements.
notable: First proposed federal rule requiring AI conflict-of-interest analysis in financial services; targets algorithmic tools that steer investors toward products benefiting the firm.
legal_citation: Release Nos. 34-97990; IA-6383 (proposed 2023)
key_obligations: Test AI/ML tools for conflicts of interest
Eliminate or neutralise identified conflicts
Disclose use of predictive analytics to investors
Maintain compliance programs for AI investment tools

impact_assessment.detail: Proposed rule requires pre-deployment testing of AI tools for conflicts of interest; documented assessment must be maintained.

prohibited_categories.detail: No prohibited AI categories; rule requires conflict neutralisation rather than prohibition.

human_review_rights.detail: No individual human review rights; compliance focus is on firm obligations.

private_right_of_action.detail: SEC enforcement only; no private right of action under the proposed rule.

synthetic_media.detail: Financial services context; does not address synthetic media.

biometric_data.detail: No biometric provisions.

training_data_transparency.detail: No training data disclosure; compliance focus is on conflict identification.

content_labeling.detail: Disclosure to investors of AI use required; not content labeling.

anti_discrimination.detail: No anti-discrimination provisions; conflict of interest focus is on investor harm, not protected class discrimination.

risk_classification.detail: No risk classification framework; conflict identification applies to all covered AI tools.

enforcement_model.detail: SEC enforcement through civil penalties, disgorgement, and injunctions; criminal referral to DOJ for wilful violations.
